Simple Portfolios that Deliver Consistent Decent Returns

Oskar Edén Wallberg1,2    Alexander Karolin1,2

February 5, 2026

Abstract

Portfolio construction has been studied extensively in both academia and industry. Its applications range from pension funds and hedge funds to private savings. The academic literature centers on methodology, commonly evaluated in settings that allow short selling, leverage, and frequent trading. Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.

1 Introduction

Portfolio construction was first formalized by Harry Markowitz in 1952 [74]. The main idea behind portfolio construction is to balance risk and reward by diversifying investments. Markowitz was able to define diversification in mathematical terms, however the concept has been known for much longer. As far back as the third century, the Talmud advised splitting wealth three ways, one in land, one in business, and one held in reserve [75]. The core concepts still apply today, and investing has grown significantly in popularity. Professional investors such as Warren Buffett and Peter Lynch diversify across tens or hundreds of investments, while quantitative hedge funds such as Citadel hold positions in thousands of different financial instruments. For the private investor, tracking such quantities of assets requires time and effort beyond what is reasonable. In this paper, we present some modern portfolio construction techniques applied to portfolios with a more manageable number of assets, making them practical for private investors to replicate and maintain.

1.1 Investing and diversification

A common problem all investors face is how to allocate their capital in a way that balances risk and return. There are many options to choose from in financial markets, including securities such as stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. A more recent addition, the exchange-traded fund (ETF), has become an increasingly popular alternative. An ETF is a fund traded like a stock, meaning that it can be bought and sold throughout the trading day, unlike a mutual fund. An ETF holds a basket of underlying assets such as stocks, bonds, or commodities, and typically tracks an index. The most traded ETF has the ticker (identifier) SPY [99], and tracks the Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500). The S&P 500 is a market index that tracks the performance of the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the US.

A long-standing fact is that it is difficult to consistently outperform a broad market index such as the S&P 500, even for professional managers [72, 91]. Warren Buffett famously bet a financial institute $1 million that no funds they selected could outperform the S&P 500, net of fees, over a 10-year period (2008–2017) [20]. Buffett won. A natural first investment is therefore to simply hold the S&P 500, e.g., via SPY. Figure 1 shows the growth of SPY over the past two decades, with an initial investment growing roughly sevenfold.

The path to a sevenfold total return is far from smooth. The average annual return of SPY over this period is 10%10\%, meaning that if you were to invest $100 at the beginning of a given year you would expect to have $110 at the end of that year. This is however just an average. In reality the return of SPY will be higher or lower for some years. In fact, the majority of the losses and gains from SPY come from a small minority of days, as seen in Figure 2.

We refer to the magnitude of these variations as the volatility, or the "riskiness" of investing in an asset. For SPY, the annual volatility is 19%19\%, meaning that the annual returns typically fall within −9%-9\% and 29%29\% (10%±19%10\%\pm 19\%) in a given year, though not always. Some years have seen extreme drawdowns such as during the Financial Crisis in 2008, the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, and the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022. The largest drawdown was during the Financial Crisis when SPY fell by 55%55\% from its peak, wiping out an estimated $7\$7 trillion of market cap in the S&P 500 [19].

One simple method for mitigating volatility and large drawdowns is to diversify investments into multiple assets that do not experience losses and gains at the same time. The most famous and very simple example of diversification is the 60/40 portfolio [36], which can be replicated with ETFs by combining SPY with AGG into a 60:40 ratio. AGG is an ETF that tracks an index of US aggregate bonds. Bonds have historically had a low or slightly negative correlation with equities such as SPY. Figure 3 shows the cumulative return of SPY, AGG, and the 60/40 portfolio over the same period.

Looking at the figure, SPY ends with the largest total return but is also the most volatile of the three. AGG, on the other hand, grows much more slowly with an average annual return of 3%3\%, but is much more stable with a volatility of 5%5\%. The 60/40 portfolio falls somewhere in between, with an average annual return of 8%8\% and a volatility of 11%11\%. The same pattern shows up in the drawdowns. During the 2008 Financial Crisis AGG only fell by 13%13\% and the 60/40 by 36%36\%, compared to SPY’s 55%55\%. By mixing in some bonds, you keep some of SPY’s long-run growth while almost halving the volatility and taking a much smaller hit during bad years. This is the value of diversification, by combining assets whose returns are mostly independent you end up with a portfolio that gives you a better balance between risk and return than either asset on its own. The trade-off between return and risk is often expressed as a ratio, formally known as the Sharpe ratio [94]. The Sharpe ratio expresses the efficiency of the portfolio and can be interpreted as return per unit of risk taken. Between 2005 and 2025 the Sharpe ratios for AGG, SPY, and 60/40 were 0.23, 0.45, and 0.51, respectively.

1.2 Quantitative trading

So far we have only looked at risk and return with one famous example of a portfolio. In practice, investing involves many more considerations. Which assets should be held, in what proportions, and when should they be bought or sold? Most private investors have no systematic framework to answer these questions, constructing their investment philosophy instead from experience and word of mouth [73, 50, 55]. Decisions made this way have historically underperformed the market [32, 7, 44]. An alternative is to make decisions systematically. One example of this is quantitative trading, where every rule is mathematically defined and decisions are computed from historical data. The investor’s job now reduces to choosing a trading strategy and following it.

To make these decisions systematically, a mathematical framework can be used. One widely used framework is the Markowitz formulation [74] expressed as a convex problem. The original Markowitz formulation models the trade-off between return and risk, and adding cost gives us a complete model for quantitative trading. A simplification of this model can be expressed as a general convex problem,

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} Return−Risk−Cost\displaystyle\text{Return}-\text{Risk}-\text{Cost}
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} Trading limits,\displaystyle\text{Trading limits},

where the return is maximized while risk and cost are minimized, subject to limits on the trades. Each of the three terms can be modeled mathematically. The risk is captured by a risk model, the return by a forecast, and the cost by a cost model. Forecasted returns are commonly known as alpha, hence the forecast is described as an alpha model. Combining the three gives a complete portfolio construction model, as in Figure 4.

Trading.

The model of Figure 4 decide what to buy at a given time, but how frequently a quantitative strategy trades varies. Some large firms utilize high frequency trading, executing trades multiple times per second, while others trade far less often. Regardless of strategy, you must trade at some frequency. Consider a simple strategy such as the 60/40 of Figure 3. Simply buying SPY and AGG in a 60:40 ratio in 2005 and never touching the portfolio would have ended 2025 at an 86:14 ratio, as seen in Figure 5, because SPY outgrew AGG. The drifted portfolio is no longer the one chosen. Its volatility in 2025 was 11%11\% against 8%8\% for the maintained version, so without trading, the risk profile walks away from what the investor intended. For a fixed weight strategy such as the 60/40, restoring the target weights, selling what has grown and buying what has lagged, is known as rebalancing. Rebalancing also carries a second benefit, in that it systematically trims positions after they have risen and adds to them after they have fallen, without any attempt to time the market. The 60/40 is a deliberately simple example, where trading only ever restores the same fixed weights. A strategy can equally well decide to move capital from one asset to another based on another heuristic than weight drifting, and the trades then serve whatever the strategy dictates.

Risk model.

In §1.1 we saw that what matters for a portfolio is not just how much each asset moves, but also how the asset returns rr move together. The risk model collects both into a single object, the covariance matrix Σ=Cov⁡(r)\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(r). For a universe of nn assets the covariance matrix is an n×nn\times n grid,

Σ=[σ12σ12⋯σ1​nσ21σ22⋯σ2​n⋱σn​1σn​2⋯σn2],\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{1}^{2}&\sigma_{12}&\cdots&\sigma_{1n}\\ \sigma_{21}&\sigma_{2}^{2}&\cdots&\sigma_{2n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \sigma_{n1}&\sigma_{n2}&\cdots&\sigma_{n}^{2}\end{bmatrix},

where each diagonal entry σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} is the variance of asset ii and each off-diagonal entry σi​j\sigma_{ij} is the covariance between assets ii and jj. Just like volatility, variance is also a measurement of risk and describes how much an asset moves on its own, while covariance describes how two assets move together. A large positive σi​j\sigma_{ij} means two assets tend to rise and fall as one, while a negative value means one tends to rise when the other falls. This is the property diversification relies on, and from this single object the risk of any portfolio can be computed.

Alpha.

The risk model describes how asset returns move together, but says nothing about where they are headed. That forecast is the job of the alpha model. Within the financial literature alpha is the expected asset returns over the next period,

αt=𝐄⁡[rt+1].\alpha_{t}=\mathbf{E}[r_{t+1}].

Within the context of Markowitz, alpha does not have to be the exact future return of the assets. Rather it can be simplified and estimation errors can be reduced using robustification techniques. Some simplifications include reducing alpha to a yes or no question, whether the return of asset A will be positive or negative tomorrow. Another simplification is forecasting only the relative order of the investable assets. Simple forecasting methods use previous returns of each asset to model future returns. However, in industry alpha is more diffuse, and can be interpreted as some information about how the prices of assets will move in the future. Examples of data that have been used to achieve alpha are satellite imagery, weather forecasts, or social media sentiment. For the curious reader, [84] gives a more thorough breakdown, best enjoyed while taking lunch.

Cost model.

Trading is not free and each trade incurs two main costs. The first is the broker fee, or commission, charged to execute the trade. The second is the bid-ask spread. At any moment an asset has two quoted prices, the bid, the highest price a buyer will pay, and the ask, the lowest price a seller will accept. The spread is the gap between them, and it is a cost to both sides. Suppose you want to sell asset A. The ask price is $101 and the bid price is $99. The effective price sits in the middle at $100, so selling at the $99 bid costs you $1 against that midpoint, half the $2 spread. Spreads are usually quoted in basis points, where one hundred basis points equal 1% of the price. A $2 spread on a $100 asset is a 200 basis point spread, and the half-spread paid by each side is 100 basis points. Figure 6 illustrates this with the common example of SPY.

The figure shows the price of SPY, with the bid and ask quoted on either side as dashed lines. The true price lies in the middle, and the distance from the midpoint to either quote is the half-spread, what a buyer or seller actually pays. Cost models can be made considerably more detailed, accounting for fees, currency conversion, and the price impact of large orders, but they are often simplified to a fixed percentage charged on the value of every trade.

1.3 Previous work

This paper is an empirical study of portfolio construction applied to a universe of ETFs. Applying systematic portfolio methods to ETFs is itself an active area of research, with recent work studying multi-asset ETF portfolios built from prediction and optimization [65], momentum and trend-following across asset classes [70], and the effect of rebalancing on ETF-only portfolios [6]. Our contribution is not a new method but a transparent application of well-established techniques to a simple, retail-accessible universe, with an emphasis on what each component contributes. Further work on the topic can be found in [devanathan:2026], which was developed in parallel within the same group at Stanford.

Portfolio construction.

The original Markowitz formulation has been studied thoroughly, and many variations exist. A few examples include the Black-Litterman model [11], robust mean-variance optimization [46], and the modern Markowitz at seventy formulation [16]. These variations were, among other reasons, developed to address the estimation sensitivity that return forecasting introduces in the original Markowitz formulation. There are however multiple methods that do not require an estimated future return. Common methods include minimum variance [30], inverse volatility [63], risk parity [87], and maximum diversification [28]. These methods instead construct portfolios based on asset risk.

Risk model.

Many portfolio construction methods require a risk model which is a covariance matrix of asset returns estimated from a rolling window of historical data. Estimating this matrix well is difficult, and a large part of current financial research goes into producing robust estimates [104, 54, 86, 24]. Using a naive sample covariance introduces multiple problems. One of the problems being that when the number of assets is large relative to the number of observations the estimate becomes unreliable. Another problem is that using large covariance matrices is computationally inefficient. One way to handle this problem is to use a factor model. Factor models have a long history. The concept of factor analysis was first introduced by Spearman in 1904 [97]. It was later adopted in finance where asset returns are modeled as being driven by a few common factors plus idiosyncratic noise. While such models date back to the single-factor CAPM [93], the framework was popularized by Fama and French, who introduced empirically tested models with multiple factors [38, 39]. Factor models are widely used today in industry [82, 4] and academia [40, 41, 61] and results in interpretable, faster and more reliable covariance estimate. Most factor models use economically interpretable factors, such as the market. An alternative is to extract factors statistically from the returns themselves, for instance through principal component analysis or related latent-factor methods [31].

Alpha.

The return forecast, or alpha, is a central part of the Markowitz formulation, and receives a great deal of attention in both academia and industry [60, 56, 8, 69]. Return prediction is difficult. The signal-to-noise ratio in financial data is extremely low, far lower than in most other domains where statistical learning is applied [68]. It is easy to overfit to noise rather than signal, and therefore it limits the complexity of the models that can be used. A common response to the low signal-to-noise ratio is regularization, which constrains the model to reduce overfitting. Examples include ridge regression [49], Laplacian-regularized models [103], and the broader use of shrinkage and sign constraints. Whether alpha prediction works is debated in academia. Goyal and Welch [47] found that a long list of popular predictors fail to beat the historical mean out of sample, while Campbell and Thompson [23] showed that the same predictors do beat it once weak restrictions are imposed. Within industry, alpha is achieved by having an edge against the market. Data and methods used to produce alpha are highly confidential and employees working with alpha prediction often have to sign long non-disclosure and non-compete agreements [110].

Software.

Software for solving optimization problems is almost as old as the methods themselves. The first nontrivial linear program ever solved took nine people around four months on hand calculators in the 1940s [10], a calculation that solvers now finish instantly.†† Throughout this project we were challenged to solve at least one billion Markowitz problems, an ambition that would have made those nine people faint. Today the field of convex optimization has matured and been adopted in many software libraries such as CVXPY for Python [35], Convex.jl for Julia [105], and CVXR for R [45]. These libraries have produced a wave of accessible portfolio optimization tools. A few examples are Portfolio Visualizer [96], PyPortfolioOpt [76], Riskfolio-Lib [22], and CVXPortfolio [21]. Their coverage varies widely, from simple web-based backtesting and visualization to specific methods such as mean-variance optimization, risk parity [67], and multi-period construction. Commercial alternatives also exist and are widely used in industry [4, 82, 14].

1.4 This paper

This paper studies portfolios that are simple, and yields consistent, and decent returns. None of the methods we use are new. Techniques are gathered from across the portfolio construction literature and industry practitioners and we apply them to one universe under one set of rules, and report what works. The rules are the same for every portfolio. We use no leverage and no shorting, target an annual volatility of 8%8\%, and earn the federal funds rate on cash. Strategies trade monthly with a 55 basis points bid-ask spread and are backtested from 2005-01-01 to 2025-01-01. We do not tune parameters to this period. The results are presented for research and educational purposes and do not constitute investment advice.

By simple we mean three things. First, the strategies are implementable. They use only public data and a small set of well-known, liquid US ETFs. Second, the math is explainable. We use no deep learning and no construction methods that are hard to interpret. We take a clear set of ETFs, divide them into asset classes, and run well-understood methods on each. Third, the parameters are interpretable. We use quantities a reader can reason about, such as a hard target-volatility constraint and turnover limits stated as percentages. If you want a higher volatility target, you change one number.

By consistent we mean a portfolio should do well across the whole period, not just in a few good years. We measure this with the Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and, as a stricter test, with the lower quantile of the twenty recorded annual Sharpe ratios. By decent we mean annual returns in the range of 6% to 10%.

We study two families of portfolios. In the first family, we make no return forecast at all. The allocation methods are fixed weights, inverse volatility, minimum volatility, risk parity, and maximum diversification, either combined across different asset classes or applied to just a few select assets. In the second family, each asset produces its own alpha signal. We combine all of these signals and solve a single Markowitz problem for each trading day. In the final section we present reasonable portfolios for the different methods we have explored.

We benchmark against the reference 60/4060/40 portfolio. A backtest over two decades can look good simply because of how a portfolio handled one or two extreme events, so we also check how sensitive our proposed portfolios are to the choice of window. Each portfolio is rerun over two truncated periods, one with the first five years removed, which excludes the Financial Crisis, and one with the last five removed, which excludes the COVID-19 pandemic and the start of the Russia-Ukraine war. If a portfolio performs well in all three windows we can consider it to be less dependent on a specific event.

Software.

Along with this paper we release three resources. The first is a web-based tool that lets readers explore the historical performance of some of the simple portfolios we construct, with interactive controls for the relevant parameters. The second is our codebase, made open source so that the strategies described can be replicated, extended, or used as a starting point for new portfolio designs. Both are available at

https://github.com/AlexEmrik/consistent-decent-returns.

The third is an open source package which lets anyone create a factor risk model through a simple python API. It is installed via

pip install covforge

Outline.

The rest of the paper follows the structure of the Markowitz formulation, from the assets it allocates across to the inputs it requires. In §2 we define the asset universe, organized into categories by asset class and underlying structure. In §3 we set up the portfolio construction problem, present the simple trading strategies and the modified Markowitz formulation we use throughout, and describe how the portfolios are selected. In §4 and §5 we cover the two inputs the strategies requires, the risk model, from simple covariance estimators to the factor model, and the return forecast, from simple alphas to ridge regression. Finally, in §6 we report the experiments, including the data, backtest, parameter choices, and results, and conclude in §7.

What we have found.

Simple strategies work surprisingly well, often performing as well as or better than more complicated approaches. Some quantitative methods for investing stand out as particularly useful. One example is volatility control, which lets the investor target a desired level of volatility. Among the simple strategies, fixed weights stand out as both effective and extremely simple given an educated selection of ETFs. Given that we are limited to open data, risk forecasting works surprisingly well while return prediction proves to be futile. However, with simple alpha signals and some robustification, Markowitz portfolio optimization is still able to deliver consistent decent returns.

2 Assets

Portfolio construction is the problem of deciding how to allocate capital across a set of assets. This section defines the universe of ETFs we invest in, organized into categories by asset class and underlying structure. From this universe the simple strategies of §3 later select portfolios of three to five ETFs, while the Markowitz formulation is given whole asset categories.

2.1 Investable universe

Our universe consists of the 59 US-listed ETFs given in Table 1, spanning the three asset classes: equities, fixed income, and alternatives. We include only large, liquid ETFs from established issuers, and exclude leveraged and inverse products, which amplify an index’s daily moves or bet against them. The ETFs themselves come in a few different kinds. Some track an index, such as SPY tracking the S&P 500, and AGG tracking a broad index of US bonds. Others hold a single asset, so their value simply follows its price. GLD holds gold and IBIT holds bitcoin. A few hold more complicated financial instruments tied to the price of an asset rather than the asset itself. We return to these in §2.2. Together the ETFs cover most of what an investor can reach with an online brokerage account. This includes several kinds of equities and bonds, commodities, and the recent addition of cryptocurrencies. Table 26 in the appendix gives a short description and summary statistics for each ETF.

Survivorship bias.

Our universe was selected from ETFs trading today, and none of the 59 were delisted during the 2005–2025 backtest window; it is therefore survivorship-biased by construction. Roughly one third of all ETFs ever launched in the US have been liquidated, with 189 closures in 2024 alone and approximately 1,550 over the preceding decade [58, 80]. However, closures concentrate disproportionately in segments excluded from our universe. The typical liquidated ETF has fewer than $50M in assets under management, a sub-five-year track record, and underperformed broad benchmarks by several percentage points in the trailing year prior to liquidation [79]. Leveraged and inverse products, which we exclude entirely, account for a closure rate of 52% versus 31% for regular ETFs [26]. We therefore expect the resulting upward bias on reported Sharpe ratios to be modest, though we do not estimate it formally.

2.2 Asset categories

Within each asset class some ETFs are structurally very different. We therefore divide the three classes further into a total of nine categories as seen in Table 2, each grouping ETFs that are similar in what they hold and how they hold it. The categorization is our own rather than an industry standard, and reflects the nature of the ETFs in our universe.

Equities.

ETFs within the Equities asset class consist of broad baskets of stocks. Simply put, owning a stock equates to owning a share of a company. Thus, owning an ETF within the Equities asset class equates to owning many small shares in different companies. We split Equities into three categories: Market, Sector, and Country.

The Market category consists of nine ETFs spanning US market-cap, style, and factor exposures [98, 13, 107, 25, 51]. ETFs in this category are generally considered good buy-and-hold investments for the investor who does not engage in active portfolio construction. They tend to yield the highest average annual returns out of the categories and perform consistently well, but suffer during market crashes. Correlation within the Market category is very high. What differs is the risk profile, with QQQ at one end having an annual volatility of 22% while USMV at the other has only 14%.

The Sector category consists of the nine original Select Sector SPDRs [100], which together divide the companies of the S&P 500 by sector [81]. All of the SPDR ETF tickers begin with XL. We complement them with two ETFs covering biotechnology and real estate [13]. The nine original SPDRs are often grouped into defensive and offensive ones. Defensive sectors, such as health care and consumer staples, are less volatile and hold up better in distressed markets. Offensive sectors, such as technology and financials, trend periodically, delivering strong returns in good years but deeper drawdowns in bad ones.

The Country category consists of fifteen ETFs, with tickers beginning with EW, each tracking an MSCI index of a single country’s equity market [12]. They cover both developed markets, such as the UK and Sweden, and emerging markets, such as Brazil and South Korea. The ETFs trade in dollars while the stocks they hold trade in each country’s own currency. They are unhedged, meaning this currency effect is not removed. The Sweden ETF EWD, for example, combines the performance of Swedish stocks with the move of the krona against the dollar, and loses value when the krona weakens even if the value of the underlying stocks is unchanged. The country ETFs are highly correlated with the US market and correlations with SPY range between 68% and 84%. Over shorter periods the country ETFs have outperformed SPY. However, over the past two decades every one of them has underperformed, with average annual returns ranging between 1% and 8% against SPY’s 10%. Figure 7 shows all fifteen ETFs together with SPY.

Fixed income.

ETFs within the Fixed income asset class consist of varying forms of bonds. A bond is a contract between the investor and an issuing institution, typically a government or a company. Investing in a bond equates to lending out money to that institution for an agreed period and receiving interest payments, known as coupons, in return. What makes bonds differ from normal loans is that the contract can be traded on the market, adding speculative value on top of the coupons and issue price. We split Fixed income into three categories depending on the type of issuer and region: Government, Corporate, and Global.

The Government category consists of five ETFs that hold bonds issued by the US government and related debt [13]. Their returns are lower than those of equities, but so is their risk. Government bond correlations with SPY are among the lowest in the investable universe, some even being negative. The negative correlation can be explained by their valuation having an inverse relationship to the federal funds rate (FFR). The FFR tends to be cut during economic downturns when equities fall. A clear example of this was the 2008 Financial Crisis. As the FFR was cut, the fixed coupons of existing bonds became more attractive than the new lower rates, causing government bond prices to rise. Long-term Treasury bonds are the most sensitive to changes in the FFR. Between 2020 and 2023 TLT, which holds 20+ year Treasuries, lost close to half of its value as the FFR rose.

The Corporate category consists of three ETFs that hold bonds issued by companies [13]. A company is less certain to repay its loans than the US government, since companies can default and go bankrupt. Corporate bonds therefore pay higher interest to attract lenders. LQD lends to large, financially strong companies, while HYG lends to weaker companies that pay the highest interest. The third ETF, LQDH, holds LQD together with a hedge that removes its interest-rate risk. Corporate bonds are more correlated with the stock market than government bonds. LQD has a correlation of 19% with SPY and HYG 68%, the highest of any bond ETF, and HYG lost roughly a third of its value in the 2008 Financial Crisis. The average annual returns in the Corporate category range from 3% to 5%, slightly above the government ETFs.

The Global category consists of four ETFs that hold bonds issued outside the US [13, 107]. BNDX and IAGG lend to developed-world governments and companies. Both are hedged, meaning the currency effect described for the Country category is removed. They have the lowest volatility of any bond ETF, 4%, and near-zero correlation with SPY. EMB and VWOB instead hold bonds issued exclusively by governments in emerging markets, such as Mexico and Brazil. These governments issue some of their bonds in US dollars, and it is those that these ETFs hold, so the money is lent and repaid in dollars and the currency effect does not apply. The interest is higher because repayment is less certain. A government that has borrowed in dollars must find dollars to repay, which becomes harder when its own currency weakens. Because of this, the volatility of EMB and VWOB is higher than that of the US government bond ETFs, at 11% and 9% respectively, and their correlation with SPY is significantly higher.

Alternatives.

The Alternatives asset class consists of ETFs that hold commodities and cryptocurrencies. These are the ETFs where structure matters most. As noted in §2.1, some hold the asset itself while others hold financial instruments tied to its price. We therefore split Alternatives by structure into three categories: Physical, Futures, and Crypto.

The Physical category consists of three ETFs that each hold a precious metal in vaults: GLD holds gold, SLV silver, and PPLT platinum [98, 13, 1]. A share corresponds to an amount of metal in the vault, so each ETF follows the spot price of its metal, less a small fee. All three are nearly uncorrelated with the rest of the universe. Among the precious metals, gold stands out. It has served as a store of value for millennia and remains a reserve asset for central banks today, and it is the only one of the three that has appreciated significantly over time. Put plainly, gold is the one physical commodity in our universe suited to buy and hold.

The Futures category consists of seven ETFs covering energy, agriculture, and industrial metals [106, 101].

As Figure 8 shows, every one of them has lost to holding plain cash earning the FFR over the backtest period, and the reason lies in how these ETFs are built. Unlike gold, these commodities are impractical to vault, so the ETFs in this category hold futures contracts. A futures contract is an agreement to buy a fixed amount of a commodity, at a fixed price, on a fixed date in the future. However, even though they could, managers of future-based ETFs never take delivery. As a contract approaches its delivery date, the fund sells it and buys a new contract with a later date, a procedure known as rolling. The later contract is usually the more expensive one, since whoever promises delivery further out must store, insure, and finance the commodity for longer and charges for it, a situation known as contango. When a futures-based ETF is in contango, the fund loses a little money on every roll, and the losses compound. Over days or weeks the ETF therefore tracks its respective commodity price closely, but over years it drifts steadily below it. These ETFs can therefore not be bought and held. They are instruments for taking commodity exposure over shorter horizons.

The Crypto category consists of two ETFs: IBIT holds bitcoin and ETHA holds ether, the two largest cryptocurrencies [13]. The Crypto ETFs are the most recently listed ETFs in the investable universe. IBIT was listed in January 2024 and ETHA in July. Their annual volatilities and returns are many times those of SPY, and both have at one point lost more than 80% of their value from an all time high. At the same time they are largely uncorrelated with the other assets in the universe. Crypto therefore requires special treatment in our experiments. Following [53], we record bitcoin and ether returns from 2017, extending the two ETFs backward with the prices of the coins they hold. This gives eight years of history rather than one. We nevertheless treat these observations with caution. Before 2024 crypto could not be reached through an ordinary brokerage account. Bitcoin has also returned over 50% per year since 2017, meaning that large allocations can easily dominate historical portfolio performance. We therefore allow Crypto in selected experiments and portfolios under §5.2, but restrict it to modest allocations so that the results do not depend disproportionately on its exceptional historical returns.

Correlation between categories.

Figure 9 shows the correlation between each of the nine categories. The three Equities categories together with corporate bonds show the highest correlation. Outside this block correlations are low.

3 Portfolio construction

Portfolio construction concerns the problem of deciding how to allocate capital across a set of assets. This section begins by introducing the notation and terminology for portfolio weights, cash, returns, and risk, objects fundamental to portfolio construction regardless of the trading strategy. Our notation is similar to that of [16]. We then present a set of common trading strategies in increasing order of complexity: fixed weights, simple optimization, and our version of the Markowitz formulation.

3.1 Mathematical model

Assets and cash weights.

We consider a universe of nn investable assets. A portfolio is described by a vector of asset weights w∈𝐑nw\in\mathbf{R}^{n}, where each weight wiw_{i} denotes the fraction of capital invested in asset ii, so wi=0.10w_{i}=0.10 corresponds to allocating 10%10\% of the portfolio to asset ii. The holdings sum to one, representing all available capital, and the fraction not invested in assets is held as cash c∈𝐑c\in\mathbf{R}. Writing 𝟏∈𝐑n\mathbf{1}\in\mathbf{R}^{n} for the vector with all entries one, and permitting neither short selling nor leverage, every portfolio in this paper satisfies the constraints

𝟏T​w+c=1,w≥0,c≥0.\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w+c=1,\qquad w\geq 0,\qquad c\geq 0.

Portfolio risk and return.

Each asset ii yields a return rir_{i} over the investment period, the fractional change in its price adjusted for dividends, splits, and other corporate actions. We collect these in the return vector r=(r1,…,rn)∈𝐑nr=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{n})\in\mathbf{R}^{n}, so that the return of a portfolio is the weighted sum rT​wr^{\mathrm{T}}w. Future returns are, however, uncertain, and the strategies of this section handle this uncertainty through two quantities, the portfolio risk and the forecasted portfolio return,

wT​Σ​w,αT​w,w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w,\qquad\alpha^{\mathrm{T}}w,

where Σ∈𝐑n×n\Sigma\in\mathbf{R}^{n\times n} is the covariance matrix of the returns and α∈𝐑n\alpha\in\mathbf{R}^{n} is a forecast of the expected asset returns. The diagonal entries Σi​i=Var⁡(ri)\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(r_{i}) of the covariance matrix hold each asset’s individual risk, how much the asset moves on its own, while the off-diagonal entries Σi​j=Cov⁡(ri,rj)\Sigma_{ij}=\operatorname{Cov}(r_{i},r_{j}) hold the covariances, how each pair of assets moves together. The vector of asset volatilities σ∈𝐑n\sigma\in\mathbf{R}^{n}, is defined as,

σi=Σi​i.\sigma_{i}=\sqrt{\Sigma_{ii}}.

The total portfolio risk is reduced either by holding lower risk assets or by holding assets with low or negative correlation, which is the diversification effect of §1.1 in mathematical form. The risk enters nearly every strategy that follows, while the forecast α\alpha is used only by the Markowitz formulation of §3.3. The estimation of both is the subject of §4 and §5, and throughout this section they are treated as known.

Optimization problem formulation.

The strategies of this section differ in how they choose the weights. The simplest methods fix ww directly, through a fixed allocation, or decide ww as a function of σ\sigma. The rest obtain ww by solving an optimization problem, which in its most general form can be written as

minimize\displaystyle\text{minimize} f0​(x)\displaystyle f_{0}(x)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} fi(x)≤0,i=1,…,m,\displaystyle f_{i}(x)\leq 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,
gi(x)=0,i=1,…,p,\displaystyle g_{i}(x)=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,p,

where xx denotes the optimization variables, f0f_{0} is the objective function, and fif_{i} and gig_{i} are inequality and equality constraints. For us the variables xx are the portfolio weights ww, the constraints are the portfolio constraints mentioned above among others, and the objective is built from the portfolio’s risk and forecasted return. All of the problems we pose are convex, which means they can be solved reliably and in fractions of a second on a standard laptop [35].

3.2 Simple trading strategies

In this section we present five simple long only strategies, following the risk-based asset allocation framework of [63]. Fixed weights (with and without volatility control), inverse volatility, minimum variance, risk parity, and maximum diversification. The first two do not use any optimization at all while the other three do.

Fixed weights.

The simplest way of choosing your portfolio weights is to use a fixed weight strategy. The fixed weight trading strategy does not require a forecast of any kind. The weights are predetermined and trading only serves to keep the weights at their desired level. Our benchmark portfolio, the 60/40, is an example of this strategy, in which the weights of SPY and AGG are fixed to w=(0.6,0.4)w=(0.6,0.4). A common general version of the fixed weight trading strategy is using equal weights. The equal weight strategy simply allocates capital equally across all nn assets as,

w=𝟏n.w=\frac{\mathbf{1}}{n}. (1)

It is well documented that the fixed weight strategy is hard to beat out of sample, because there is nothing in it to misestimate [33].

Volatility control.

Fixed weights control risk only implicitly, through the choice of assets but the actual risk of the portfolio is whatever the market delivers and changes over time. The 60/40 realized an average volatility of 8% over the past two decades, but roughly 23% during the 2008 Financial Crisis. Volatility control is a method that makes risk explicit, by treating cash as a risk-free asset and scaling down its positions in the portfolio so that the estimated volatility stays below a chosen target risk σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}. Scaling the weights ww by a factor θ\theta and holding the rest as cash scales the portfolio volatility by the same factor, so the target is met by holding θ​w\theta w in assets and c=1−𝟏T​θ​wc=1-\mathbf{1}^{T}\theta w in cash, with

θ=σtgtwT​Σ​w,\theta=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}}{\sqrt{w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w}}, (2)

capped at θ=1\theta=1 since we do not permit leverage. The portfolio is thus fully invested in calm markets and moves partly to cash in turbulent ones. This turns risk into an interpretable parameter. Investors who want a portfolio with a maximum risk of 8%8\% simply set σtgt=8%\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}=8\%.

Inverse volatility.

The inverse-volatility portfolio sizes each position relative to its own risk, so that every asset contributes a similar amount of volatility to the portfolio [63, 64],

w=σ−1𝟏T​σ−1.w=\frac{\sigma^{-1}}{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\sigma^{-1}}. (3)

Lower risk assets therefore occupy larger holdings. Take the 60/40 as an example. SPY carries an annual volatility of 19%19\% against AGG’s 5%5\%, so despite the 60/40 split of capital, nearly all of the portfolio’s movement comes from SPY. Sized by inverse volatility instead, the same two assets would roughly be split as 20%20\% SPY and 80%80\% AGG. The weights use only each asset’s individual volatility and ignore correlations. When the assets are uncorrelated, or share the same pairwise correlation, inverse volatility coincides with the risk parity strategy later in this chapter [71], but when correlations differ it misjudges the risk, since an asset that moves with the rest of the portfolio contributes more than its own volatility suggests. For this reason it is also known as naive risk parity [95]. Its simplicity keeps it popular in practice, and the rule is applied across asset classes [63, 64, 95].

Minimum volatility.

The minimum volatility portfolio minimizes the total portfolio variance subject to being fully invested and our long-only constraints [30],

minimize𝑤\displaystyle\underset{w}{\text{minimize}} wT​Σ​w\displaystyle w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w (4)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Tw=1,w≥0.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w=1,\quad w\geq 0.

Minimum volatility is a cash free strategy, since cash is assumed to be risk free the strategy would simply collapse into cash only. It uses the full covariance matrix, so it can exploit assets that offset one another. However, with no notion of return, it concentrates capital in the assets with the lowest volatility. For example, in an investable universe that includes stable but low-yielding bonds, the minimum volatility portfolio invests almost exclusively in the bonds, accepting very low returns in exchange for low risk. Despite this, minimum volatility portfolios have historically delivered returns comparable to the broad market at considerably lower risk [30, 5]. The strategy is behind one of the ETFs in our own universe: USMV, the ETF that individually has the highest Sharpe ratio in the Market category, holding a minimum volatility portfolio of US large- and mid-cap stocks [13].

Risk parity.

The risk parity strategy penalizes each asset not only for its own volatility but for its covariance with the rest of the portfolio. As a result, two assets with the same volatility can receive different weights if their correlations with the rest of the portfolio differ. Unlike inverse volatility, weights are formed such that each asset holding contributes equally to the total portfolio risk [88]. This equal risk contribution (ERC) condition can be expressed through the following convex formulation [71],

minimize𝑤\displaystyle\underset{w}{\text{minimize}} 12​wT​Σ​w−ρ​ 1T​log⁡(w)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w-\rho\,\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\log(w) (5)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Tw+c=1,w>0,c≥0,\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w+c=1,\quad w>0,\quad c\geq 0,

where the regularization parameter ρ>0\rho>0 balances the two objectives of minimizing portfolio risk and having a similar split between assets. When ρ=0\rho=0 it degenerates into minimum volatility as in (4), and for ρ≫0\rho\gg 0 the solution collapses into equal weights as in (1). The logarithmic term forces every weight to stay strictly positive, causing all assets to be held to some degree throughout the entire investing period. When all asset pairs share the same covariance the ERC weights coincide with the inverse volatility portfolio of (3). This is why inverse volatility has been called the naive risk parity [71]. Risk parity was popularized in conjunction with the All Weather portfolio of Bridgewater Associates [18] and has since become a standard investment strategy among institutional investors [89, 3, 27].

Maximum diversification.

The maximum diversification portfolio directly targets the reduction in portfolio risk that comes from combining assets. It does so by maximizing the diversification ratio, defined as the weighted average of the individual asset volatilities divided by the volatility of the portfolio they form. The ratio equals one for a single asset and increases as less correlated assets are combined, making it a natural measure of the diversification effect discussed in §1.1. The standard formulation of the Most Diversified Portfolio (MDP), introduced by [28], is

maximize𝑤\displaystyle\underset{w}{\text{maximize}} wT​σwT​Σ​w\displaystyle\frac{w^{\mathrm{T}}\sigma}{\sqrt{w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w}} (6)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Tw=1,w≥0.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w=1,\quad w\geq 0.

With the long-only constraint w≥0w\geq 0, the problem generally does not admit a closed-form solution. It can instead be reformulated as the convex quadratic program (QP)

minimize𝑦\displaystyle\underset{y}{\text{minimize}} yT​C​y\displaystyle y^{\mathrm{T}}Cy (7)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Ty=1,y≥0,\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y=1,\quad y\geq 0,

where yy are the portfolio weights expressed on a volatility-scaled basis and CC is the correlation matrix of returns. The full derivation is given in Appendix A. The MDP is closely related to the minimum volatility portfolio of (4) and the inverse volatility portfolio of (3), and coincides with each under particular conditions [29]. When all assets have the same volatility, MDP coincides with minimum volatility. When all asset pairs have the same correlation, MDP instead coincides with inverse volatility. In the general case, it accounts for both differences in individual volatilities and differences in correlations, making it especially relevant when the correlation structure contains meaningful cross-sectional variation. Its theoretical appeal is that if all assets offer the same expected excess return per unit of standalone risk, the MDP also maximizes the portfolio Sharpe ratio [29]. It can therefore be viewed as extending the intuition of inverse volatility by incorporating the correlation structure explicitly.

3.3 Markowitz

The simple strategies of §3.2 all assume no knowledge of future returns. Suppose instead you have a belief about how your assets will perform, e.g. that your equities will outperform your fixed income assets, or even an exact figure for each asset produced by a forecast. A natural extension of a method like minimum volatility is then to not only minimize risk but also maximize expected return. This exact trade-off was formalized by Markowitz [74] in 1952. The work was recognized with the 1990 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences [102], and still underpins portfolio allocation today, both in academia [59, 57, 16] and in industry [82, 4, 14]. At its core the idea is simple: collect the expected returns in a vector α\alpha, and maximize the return it implies for your portfolio while weighing that against the portfolio risk. The problem can be expressed in several ways. We present two standard formulations, followed by the modified version we use throughout this paper.

Formulated with a soft risk constraint.

One way to express the trade-off is to subtract the portfolio risk from the expected return in the objective, scaled by a risk-aversion parameter γ>0\gamma>0,

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} αT​w−γ​wT​Σ​w\displaystyle\alpha^{\mathrm{T}}w-\gamma\,w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w (8)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Tw+c=1,c≥0,w≥0.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w+c=1,\quad c\geq 0,\quad w\geq 0.

The parameter γ\gamma is a trade-off parameter between the two objective terms and is used to decide how much variance the investor is willing to accept per unit of expected return. A small γ\gamma tolerates more risk, while a large γ\gamma does the opposite. As γ\gamma approaches zero the penalty disappears and the solver puts everything into the single asset with the highest expected return, and as γ\gamma grows the penalty dominates until the portfolio only holds cash.

Formulated with a hard risk constraint.

The alternative is to take risk out of the objective and impose it as a constraint with a target volatility σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}},

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} αT​w\displaystyle\alpha^{\mathrm{T}}w (9)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Tw+c=1,c≥0,w≥0,\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w+c=1,\quad c\geq 0,\quad w\geq 0,
wT​Σ​w≤σtgt2.\displaystyle w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}^{2}.

Because cash can always be held, any target volatility is reachable, and the optimizer simply scales down its weights with cash until the constraint is met. The target volatility works as an upper limit, in the same way as the volatility control of (2) and realized volatility will sit close to σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}} except if the inherent risk of the portfolio is below that of σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}. One example of this would be using very large σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}} for a portfolio of low risk bond ETFs. Both formulations describe the same trade-off and can produce the same portfolios, so nothing is lost by choosing one over the other. What differs is the parameter you have to set. An investor who wants at most 8%8\% risk sets σtgt=8%\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}=8\%. However, the value of γ\gamma that yields that same portfolio cannot be predetermined, and since it depends on the scale of α\alpha it has to be adjusted if the asset universe changes. For the sake of interpretability we therefore use the hard risk constraint formulation in our extended version below.

In this paper.

Throughout this paper we use a modified version of the Markowitz formulation, similar to that of [16]. In its original form the problem responds sharply to the return forecast, and small changes in α\alpha produce large changes in the weights [78, 9, 33]. This is particularly important since, as mentioned in §1.3, α\alpha is very difficult to estimate. We define our modified Markowitz formulation as,

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} αT​w−κ​‖w−wpre‖1\displaystyle\alpha^{\mathrm{T}}w-\kappa\,\|w-w_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{1} (10)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏T​w+c=1,c≥0,w≥0\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w+c=1,\quad c\geq 0,\quad w\geq 0
wTΣw≤σtgt2,∥w−wpre∥1≤Ttgt,\displaystyle w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}^{2},\quad\|w-w_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{1}\leq T_{\mathrm{tgt}},
|w−wpre|≤δw,0≤w≤wmax,\displaystyle|w-w_{\mathrm{pre}}|\leq\delta_{w},\quad 0\leq w\leq w_{\mathrm{max}},

where wprew_{\mathrm{pre}} are the weights before trading and κ\kappa is the trading cost, a small percentage charged on every dollar bought or sold. Since ‖w−wpre‖1\|w-w_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{1} is the total amount traded, the penalty κ​‖w−wpre‖1\kappa\|w-w_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{1} represents the total cost for a given trade. The caps TtgtT_{\mathrm{tgt}} and δw\delta_{w} limit how much of the portfolio, and how much of any single position, may change in one trade. Without them a negative entry in α\alpha would empty that entire position in one trade, which is a drastic response to a number we know to be noisy. Finally wmaxw_{\mathrm{max}} limits the size of any single holding, which lets an investor cap exposure to an asset regardless of how attractive its forecast looks, for example holding crypto at no more than a few percent of the portfolio.

Regret bound.

As an upper bound on achievable performance, we also report a regret bound strategy that uses realized future returns as the alpha forecast in the Markowitz formulation [17]. This strategy is not implementable in practice but bounds the performance any return-forecasting model could achieve given the same risk model and constraints. Frequent trading while knowing future returns leads to unreasonably high Sharpe ratios. Therefore, the regret bound is only allowed to trade yearly to keep the comparison on a reasonable scale against implementable strategies.

3.4 Portfolio selection

Simple strategies.

The simple strategies can all be run on the full universe, but the result would not be a portfolio anyone would hold. Spreading capital equally across all 59 assets assumes every one of them is worth holding for two decades. It also lets the composition of the universe decide the allocation, since 35 of the 59 assets are equities the portfolio would hold roughly 60%60\% equities by construction, a split we never chose. We therefore run the simple strategies on small portfolios instead. Backtests are fast, so under the simplest strategies we search every combination of three, four, and five ETFs, less for a single winner than for what the top portfolios share, which asset classes they draw from, in what proportions, and which assets never appear. The simple optimization-based strategies are then examined further on portfolios found from these tests.

Markowitz.

Markowitz needs no such selection. It is built for large universes, and the optimizer allocates capital on its own, with the forecasted α\alpha deciding what it holds. The one selection left is at the category level. If the forecast cannot extract information from an entire category, it is better removed, which we evaluate through an ablation test in §6.3.

4 Risk model

Portfolio construction requires an estimate of future risk. While future market conditions cannot be observed directly, historical returns contain information about the volatility of individual assets and how they tend to move together, and a risk model uses this information to estimate the covariance structure that will prevail over the period for which the portfolio is constructed. This section explains what a risk model is and how the covariance is forecast from historical returns. We present two simple estimators, the rolling-window sample covariance and the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA), followed by a more sophisticated approach based on a statistical factor model.

4.1 Risk forecasting

Risk forecasting is concerned with estimating the covariance matrix Σ\Sigma, which describes both the variability of individual assets and their co-movement. Following the original formulation of [74], diversification arises from the covariance structure between assets, making an accurate estimate of Σ\Sigma central to nearly every portfolio construction method. A useful way for the reader to think about the covariance matrix is simply as

Σ−encodes future “riskiness” of assets.\Sigma-\text{encodes future ``riskiness'' of assets.}

The rolling-window and EWMA estimators are procedural approaches to covariance estimation. Both construct a risk forecast by aggregating observed historical returns according to a predetermined rule, require few assumptions, and are straightforward to implement.

The statistical factor model is particularly useful for large investment universes, where estimating every pairwise relationship directly becomes increasingly difficult. It introduces several important mathematical concepts, including statistical factors, regularization, and expectation maximization. These methods require a somewhat heavier mathematical treatment, and are deferred to Appendix A, where the reader can find details about the derivations. To keep the main discussion intuitive and readable, the focus here is on the structure of the factor model, why it is useful, and how its resulting covariance estimate should be interpreted.

4.2 Simple covariance estimators

Although the future covariance matrix cannot be observed directly, historical asset returns provide valuable information about how assets tend to move together. A covariance estimator summarizes these historical relationships into a single matrix that serves as our best estimate of future risk. Figure 10 illustrates the general covariance estimation process.

While no estimator can predict future market conditions perfectly, even simple statistical models often produce estimates that are sufficiently accurate for portfolio construction. Historical returns are collected in the return matrix Rt∈𝐑T×nR_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{T\times n}, and a covariance estimator transforms these observations into an estimated covariance matrix Σ^t∈𝐑n×n\hat{\Sigma}_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n\times n}. We represent the estimator abstractly as a mathematical function,

Σt+h≈Σ^t=f⁡(Rt),\Sigma_{t+h}\approx\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=f(R_{t}),

where the unknown future covariance matrix Σt+h\Sigma_{t+h} is approximated by the estimate Σ^t\hat{\Sigma}_{t} constructed from the historical return matrix RtR_{t}. Different covariance estimators correspond to different choices of the function f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), each making different statistical assumptions about the observed returns. Throughout this section we will introduce several increasingly sophisticated choices of f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), all of which map the same historical return matrix RtR_{t} to an estimate of future risk. Here, TT denotes the number of historical return observations contained in RtR_{t}, while nn denotes the number of assets in the investment universe.

Regardless of the estimator, they all seek to approximate the same underlying quantity: the future covariance matrix Σt+h\Sigma_{t+h}. Throughout this paper we assume zero-mean daily returns, 𝐄⁡[r]=0\mathbf{E}[r]=0, under which the covariance matrix equals the second moment,

Σ=𝐄⁡[r​rT],\Sigma=\mathbf{E}[rr^{\mathrm{T}}],

which must be estimated from a finite sample of historical returns. Different covariance estimators differ primarily in how they weight and summarize these observations. In this section we cover two simple but widely used estimators: the rolling-window sample covariance and the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) [52].

Rolling window estimate.

The simplest choice of the covariance estimator f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is the uniformly weighted sample covariance. The underlying assumption is that the average covariance observed over the most recent L trading days provides a reasonable estimate of the covariance over the future forecasting horizon. In other words, the expected future risk is approximated by the sample average of the most recent observations, with each day receiving equal weight. Also that each observation within this lookback window is equally informative when forecasting future risk. The covariance forecast is therefore obtained by averaging the pairwise products of the historical asset returns,

Σ^t=1L​RtT​Rt,\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=\frac{1}{L}R_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}R_{t}, (11)

where Rt=[rt−1,rt−2,…,rt−L]T∈𝐑L×nR_{t}=[r_{t-1},r_{t-2},\ldots,r_{t-L}]^{\mathrm{T}}\in\mathbf{R}^{L\times n} contains the trailing return observations over a lookback period of LL trading days. Figure 11 illustrates this computation graphically.

Each column of RtR_{t} corresponds to the historical returns over LL days for one asset. The matrix multiplication RtT​RtR_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}R_{t} computes the pairwise covariance between every asset in the universe, producing an n×nn\times n covariance matrix. The factor 1/L1/L normalizes these accumulated products to adjust the covariance estimates to a daily scale.

The choice of the lookback window LL reflects a trade-off between estimation accuracy and responsiveness to changing market conditions. A short lookback adapts quickly to changes in volatility and correlation, but produces a noisier covariance estimate because it is based on fewer observations. Conversely, a longer lookback reduces estimation noise by averaging over more observations, but may incorporate outdated return relationships that are no longer relevant for forecasting future risk. The faster market conditions change, the shorter LL should generally be to avoid placing excessive weight on stale data. Consequently, there is no universally optimal choice of LL, and its value depends on both the forecasting horizon hh and the persistence of the underlying covariance structure. Another limitation of the rolling-window estimator is that every observation within the lookback window receives exactly the same weight, so a return observed yesterday influences the estimate just as much as a return observed LL days ago, until it abruptly leaves the window altogether.

The choice of LL is also constrained by the number of assets nn. When L≤nL\leq n, the estimated covariance matrix is guaranteed to be rank deficient, implying the existence of zero-risk portfolios that do not exist in the true market. Even when LL is only slightly larger than nn, the covariance matrix may remain poorly conditioned and numerically unstable , so in practice L≫nL\gg n is generally preferred. For large investment universes, of say n=1000n=1000 assets, this would require multi-year lookback windows, which both increases computational cost and incorporates progressively more outdated market information.

EWMA covariance estimate.

Another widely used choice of the covariance estimator f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA). Rather than assigning equal importance to every historical return within a fixed lookback window, the EWMA estimator assigns exponentially decreasing weights to older observations. Consequently, recent market movements have a greater influence on the covariance forecast, while older observations continue to contribute with gradually diminishing weight. The covariance forecast is computed as

Σ^t=1ηt​RtT​Wt​Rt,\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\,R_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}W_{t}R_{t}, (12)

where Rt=[rt−1,rt−2,…,r1]∈𝐑(t−1)×nR_{t}=[r_{t-1},r_{t-2},\ldots,r_{1}]\in\mathbf{R}^{(t-1)\times n} contains all historical return observations available up to day t−1t-1. Figure 12 illustrates this computation.

Unlike the rolling-window estimator, which only considers the most recent LL observations, the EWMA estimator uses the entire return history while gradually reducing the influence of older observations through the diagonal weighting matrix

Wt=diag⁡(λt−1,λt−2,…,λ1).W_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{t-1},\lambda_{t-2},\ldots,\lambda_{1}).

Each diagonal entry λi\lambda_{i} along the diagonal of WW specifies the weight assigned to one historical return observation rir_{i}. Since WtW_{t} is diagonal, every row of RtR_{t} is weighted independently before the pairwise covariances are computed. The normalization constant ηt\eta_{t} is given by the sum of the EWMA weights, ensuring that the covariance estimate remains on the same scale regardless of the number of observations.

The observation weights are parameterized through a half-life HH, measured in trading days. Rather than specifying every weight individually, the weights are generated according to the exponential decay λτ=0.5τ/H\lambda_{\tau}=0.5^{\tau/H}, where τ\tau denotes the age of the observation in days. Consequently, an observation that is HH days old receives half the weight of the most recent observation, while older observations receive progressively smaller weights. The half-life therefore provides an intuitive way of controlling how quickly historical information loses influence. Smaller values of HH place greater emphasis on recent observations, whereas larger values retain information from a longer history.

Unlike the rolling-window estimator, EWMA never discards observations abruptly. Instead, every historical return continues to contribute to the covariance estimate, with its influence gradually fading as it becomes older. Since the estimator uses the entire available return history, numerical stability is determined primarily by the total number of available observations rather than by a fixed lookback window. In practice, provided that sufficiently many observations are available, typically t−1≫nt-1\gg n, the covariance estimate remains full rank while avoiding the abrupt discontinuities introduced by a rolling window. Reported half-life values range from a few days to several hundred days depending on the intended application [66, 85, 15]. Another practical advantage of EWMA is that the covariance estimate can be updated recursively as new return observations become available,

Σ^t=λ1​Σ^t−1+(1−λ1)​rt−1​rt−1T,\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=\lambda_{1}\hat{\Sigma}_{t-1}+(1-\lambda_{1})r_{t-1}r_{t-1}^{\mathrm{T}},

rather than being recomputed from the entire return history each day. This makes the EWMA estimator computationally efficient while still incorporating all previously observed market information.

4.3 Factor models

The covariance estimators introduced above estimate how every pair of assets moves together. This works well when the number of assets is small relative to the amount of historical data available. As the investment universe grows, however, the number of relationships that must be estimated grows quickly. For nn assets, the covariance matrix contains n⁡(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2 distinct pairwise covariances. With 1,000 assets, this already amounts to almost half a million relationships, all estimated from the same finite history of returns. Many of these estimates will inevitably reflect noise rather than persistent relationships in the market.

Factor models address this problem by imposing structure on how assets are allowed to move together. Rather than estimating every relationship independently, a factor model assumes that much of the co-movement between assets can be explained by a small number of common sources of variation, called factors. For example, two equity ETFs may move together not because their relationship is unique, but because both respond to the same broad movement in the equity market. If many assets share such common movements, it can be more reliable to estimate these underlying factors than every pairwise relationship separately.

There are two common ways to define these factors [24]. Economic factor models specify them explicitly, using interpretable quantities such as the market, size, and value factors of Fama and French [38, 39]. Statistical factor models instead infer the common movements directly from observed asset returns. We use the latter approach, so the factors need not have an economic interpretation. However, the first factor tends to capture the market movement. The factor model we use follows the form of [24] and is given by,

rt=Ft​ft+ϵt.r_{t}=F_{t}f_{t}+\epsilon_{t}. (13)

Figure 13 illustrates the factor model geometrically. The matrix Ft∈𝐑n×kF_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n\times k} is called the factor loading matrix, but can simply be understood as a collection of weights: each row corresponds to one asset and describes how sensitive that asset is to each of the kk factor returns. Each entry of ft∈𝐑kf_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{k} is the return of one common factor. The product Ft​ftF_{t}f_{t} therefore combines the factor returns according to the sensitivities to produce the factor-driven return of each asset.

This is essentially the familiar linear relation y=m​x+by=mx+b in vectorized form, with FtF_{t} playing the role of the slopes, ftf_{t} the explanatory variables, and ϵt∈𝐑n\epsilon_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n} the remaining unexplained component. The number of factors kk is a hyperparameter, which we elaborate on in the following part.

Factor covariance estimate.

Earlier we introduced a covariance estimator as a function f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) that maps the historical return matrix RtR_{t} to a covariance estimate Σ^t\hat{\Sigma}_{t}. For the simple estimators above, this mapping could be written in a single equation, whereas the factor model requires several intermediate steps. The factor model r=F​f+ϵr=Ff+\epsilon in (13) is an assumption about the structure of asset returns which lets us derive the decomposed form of the covariance matrix in (14), later used to construct the covariance estimate. The full estimation procedure involves volatility scaling, winsorization, EWMA correlation estimation, eigendecomposition, and expectation maximization (EM). We leave these mathematical details to Appendix A and focus here on the resulting covariance estimate and its interpretation.

The assumption in (13) has a useful consequence for the covariance matrix. The term F​fFf captures the returns explained by the common factors, while ϵ\epsilon captures the remaining asset-specific returns. If these two components are unrelated, their contributions to risk can also be separated. We therefore assume that the asset-specific returns are uncorrelated with the common factors and with each other, so that any co-movement between assets is only explained through the common factors. We also normalize the factors to have unit covariance. Under these assumptions, the covariance estimate takes the decomposed form

Σ^t=Ft​FtT+Dt,\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=F_{t}F_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}+D_{t}, (14)

where Ft​FtTF_{t}F_{t}^{\mathrm{T}} captures the covariance explained by the common factors and Dt∈𝐑n×nD_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n\times n} is a diagonal matrix containing the remaining asset-specific variances. Figure 14 illustrates how these two components combine to form the covariance estimate.

The important distinction from the simple covariance estimators is that the off-diagonal relationships are no longer estimated independently. Instead, they must be explained through the kk common factors. When k≪nk\ll n, this substantially reduces the flexibility of the model: rather than estimating 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) covariance relationships, the common covariance structure is described by the 𝒪⁡(n​k)\mathcal{O}(nk) entries of FF. This acts as a form of regularization. Relationships supported by common movements across many assets are retained, while isolated relationships caused primarily by sampling noise are less likely to enter the covariance estimate. The resulting estimate can therefore be more robust when the number of assets is large relative to the available data [62]. For large asset universes, the resulting low-rank structure can also substantially reduce computational cost.

The factor model equation in (13) and the covariance decomposition in (14) provide complementary views of the same underlying structure:

total asset returns𝑟⟵common factor-driven partF​f+asset-specific partϵ,\underset{r}{\text{total asset returns}}\longleftarrow\underset{Ff}{\text{common factor-driven part}}+\underset{\epsilon}{\text{asset-specific part}},
total asset riskΣ^⟵common factor-driven partF​FT+asset-specific part𝐷.\underset{\hat{\Sigma}}{\text{total asset risk}}\longleftarrow\underset{FF^{\mathrm{T}}}{\text{common factor-driven part}}+\underset{D}{\text{asset-specific part}}.

The factor model equation separates asset returns into movements shared across the investment universe and movements specific to individual assets. The covariance decomposition carries this same structure over to risk: F​FTFF^{\mathrm{T}} captures the risk arising from shared movements, while DD captures the remaining risk specific to each asset. Consequently, co-movement between different assets is explained through the common factors. The factor model therefore reduces a large covariance estimation problem to estimating a small set of shared movements, how strongly each asset responds to them, and whatever risk remains is attributed as specific to each asset.

5 Alpha model

Markowitz portfolio optimization requires, outside of the risk estimate, also some estimate of the future attractiveness of investments. An alpha model attempts to summarize the information contained in historical data into such a forecast. This section explains what an alpha model is and how a return forecast is constructed from historical prices. We present two simple signals, momentum and a moving average, followed by a fitted model that uses ridge regression.

5.1 Return forecasting

Return forecasting is concerned with estimating α\alpha, meant to capture the performance of investments over the coming investing period. Unlike risk, returns generally exhibit much weaker statistical structure, making useful alpha estimation considerably more difficult [77, 47]. Following the terminology of Grinold and Kahn [48], alpha is often introduced as a forecast of expected excess return. Throughout this paper, however, it is helpful to adopt a slightly broader interpretation as,

α−encodes future “goodness” of assets.\alpha-\text{encodes future ``goodness'' of assets.}

The attractiveness of an investment can be captured through many different signals, as shown in Figure 15, of which we focus on trend and reversion in this paper.

Momentum and the moving-average signal are procedural alphas constructed directly from historical prices. Both apply predetermined rules to recently observed price movements and carry the resulting information forward as an indication of future attractiveness. They require no fitted statistical model, are straightforward to implement, and provide an intuitive starting point.

Statistical return forecasting instead estimates the relationship between information available today and subsequently realized returns from historical data. This provides a considerably more flexible framework: rather than specifying beforehand how a particular signal should translate into alpha, a statistical model attempts to learn that relationship from the data. However, any forecasting model is ultimately constrained by the data it has access to. Institutional investors may combine sophisticated statistical models with proprietary datasets, alternative information, or other signals unavailable to the average market participant. Our objective is different. We restrict the forecasting problem to public, historically observable market data so that the resulting models remain reproducible and accessible. The regression models introduced later should therefore only be viewed as increasingly flexible methods for extracting whatever predictive information is present in the available features.

5.2 Simple alphas

There are countless ways to construct an alpha signal from historical market data. Prices and returns can be aggregated and transformed in many ways, producing a jungle of possible signals. The purpose of this section is not to exhaustively search for the best-performing alpha. Instead, we consider two simple and interpretable textbook alphas to investigate whether useful information can be extracted from recent prices: momentum, which retains the magnitude of recent returns, and a moving-average signal, which reduces the forecast to the direction of the recent price trend.

Momentum.

The simplest alpha we consider is momentum, where the return over a recent period is carried forward directly as the forecast. An asset that has recently appreciated receives a positive alpha, while an asset that has declined receives a negative one. The minimal underlying assumption is that price movements exhibit some persistence, such that assets performing well relative to their recent history may continue to do so over the near future. We use one-month momentum, computed from the log return over the preceding LL trading days,

momt=log⁡(pt−1pt−L)=∑τ=t−Lt−1log⁡(rτ),\mathrm{mom}_{t}=\log\!\left(\frac{p_{t-1}}{p_{t-L}}\right)=\sum_{\tau=t-L}^{t-1}\log(r_{\tau}), (15)

where pt−1p_{t-1} is the most recently observed price and pt−Lp_{t-L} is the price LL trading days earlier. Their log ratio is the continuously compounded return over the lookback period, so the signal preserves both direction and magnitude. Momentum is inherently backward-looking and reacts slowly to changes, progressively tilting the portfolio toward or away from an asset rather than attempting to anticipate the turning point itself. The lookback LL controls the trade-off between reactivity and stability. Short windows react quicker to changing trends but are more exposed to short-term noise, while longer windows produce smoother signals but respond more slowly when conditions change.

Moving average.

The moving-average signal instead reduces the alpha to a directional forecast. Rather than extrapolating the magnitude of recent returns, the signal asks only whether the current price lies sufficiently above or below its recent trend. Letting LL denote the lookback window, we define

movt=2×(pt>ρL​∑τ=t−Lt−1pτ)−1,\mathrm{mov}_{t}=2\times\mathbf{1}\!\left(p_{t}>\frac{\rho}{L}\sum_{\tau=t-L}^{t-1}p_{\tau}\right)-1, (16)

where the trailing average provides a slowly moving reference level for the current price and ρ\rho controls the threshold required to classify the trend as positive. For example, with L=50L=50 and ρ=1.2\rho=1.2 the alpha only gives a buy signal when the price is 20% above the 50-day moving average. The signal takes only two values, +1+1 when the price is sufficiently above its trailing average and −1-1 otherwise, so unlike momentum, the distance from the average carries no additional information. The signal therefore acts as a simple gate, participating while the price remains in a favorable trend and moving away as soon as that trend disappears.
