Since the current price is compared directly with the slower-moving reference, the signal reacts more quickly than momentum.

5.3 Regression models

Returning to the textbook definition of alpha as an expected future return, we can construct a set of features available at day tt and estimate how these features have historically related to returns over the subsequent horizon of hh days. The fitted relationship can then be applied to the information available today to produce a return forecast r^t+h\hat{r}_{t+h}, which is used directly, or after some transformation, as the alpha supplied to Markowitz. This turns alpha forecasting into a conventional supervised learning problem, but an unusually difficult one.

Features and dataset.

Any return forecasting model is ultimately limited by the information made available to it. We restrict this information to public and historically observable market data, keeping the forecasts reproducible and consistent with the simple investment framework considered throughout this paper. Letting ptp_{t} denote the price of asset ii at day tt,

xt(S,L)=log⁡(pt−Spt−L),x^{(S,L)}_{t}=\log\!\left(\frac{p_{t-S}}{p_{t-L}}\right), (17)

is a feature analogous to the simple momentum alpha mentioned in §5.2 with the two lookback parameters SS and LL. Here, xi,t(S,L)x^{(S,L)}_{i,t} is a data feature which covers the period between t−Lt-L to t−St-S, thus a window of L−SL-S days. With the addition of the parameter SS we are able to create a dataset of features covering non-overlapping periods of historical returns. The three very simple and classical textbook features we use in our experiments are,

STRt=−log⁡(pt−1pt−21),MTMt=log⁡(pt−21pt−252),LTRt=−log⁡(pt−252pt−756),\mathrm{STR}_{t}=-\log\!\left(\frac{p_{t-1}}{p_{t-21}}\right),\qquad\mathrm{MTM}_{t}=\log\!\left(\frac{p_{t-21}}{p_{t-252}}\right),\qquad\mathrm{LTR}_{t}=-\log\!\left(\frac{p_{t-252}}{p_{t-756}}\right), (18)

where STR is the short-term reversal feature, MTM is the medium-term momentum feature, and LTR is the long-term reversal features, also shown in Figure 16.

The reversal effect is captured by the minus signs, and is based on the assumption that the future price will move in the opposite direction of the short- and long-term trends. For each asset ii in the asset universe we form a dataset X∈𝐑T×3X\in\mathbf{R}^{T\times 3} consisting of the three aforementioned features, specific to that asset. That dataset is then used in a rolling window fashion to backtest the regression model while producing an alpha over the period 2005–2025.

Return predictability.

Predicting returns is difficult not because statistical models cannot fit historical financial data, but because there is very little persistent signal to fit. A useful way to conceptualize a future return is as the sum of a component that can, in principle, be inferred from information available today and a component that cannot,

rt+h=f⁡(Xt)+εt+h,r_{t+h}=f(X_{t})+\varepsilon_{t+h}, (19)

where f⁡(Xt)f(X_{t}) represents the predictable component contained in the feature vector XtX_{t}, while εt+h\varepsilon_{t+h} collects the remaining unpredictable variation. For financial returns, the central difficulty is that the latter is generally much larger than the former,

Var⁡[f⁡(Xt)]≪Var⁡[εt+h].\operatorname{Var}\left[f(X_{t})\right]\ll\operatorname{Var}\left[\varepsilon_{t+h}\right]. (20)

The signal-to-noise ratio is consequently very low. Even a model that estimates f⁡(Xt)f(X_{t}) reasonably well can therefore produce forecasts that appear weak when compared with individual realized returns, since each realization remains dominated by εt+h\varepsilon_{t+h}. This weak dependence is already visible in the return series themselves. If past returns contained strong information about future returns, substantial dependence would remain across nearby lags. For broad and liquid assets such as SPY, however, return autocorrelations tend to be small, leaving comparatively little structure for a forecasting model to exploit. Figure 17 illustrates this through the autocorrelation function (ACF) of SPY returns across successive lags.

Low signal-to-noise also changes how model complexity should be viewed. A flexible model has more freedom to discover relationships in the training data, but when most historical variation is noise, it also has more freedom to explain patterns that occurred by chance. A good in-sample fit can therefore be obtained without learning a relationship that persists out of sample. This is the familiar bias–variance trade-off, but it becomes particularly important for return forecasting. Reducing model bias by adding flexibility can quickly increase estimation variance as the model adapts to noise. Model complexity is therefore not automatically an advantage. The objective is instead to use enough flexibility to capture the weak systematic component of returns while restricting the model sufficiently that random historical variation is not mistaken for persistent structure.

Ridge regression.

We use a linear model to estimate the relationship between the features and subsequent returns. For a feature vector xt∈𝐑Fx_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{F}, holding the FF features observed at day tt, the return over the following hh days is modeled as

r^t+h=xtT​θ,\hat{r}_{t+h}=x_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}\theta, (21)

where θ∈𝐑F\theta\in\mathbf{R}^{F} contains one coefficient for each feature. Each coefficient describes the direction and magnitude of the estimated relationship between its feature and the return that follows. This makes the model transparent, since the contribution of every feature to a forecast can be read directly from its coefficient.

Every asset is given its own model, fitted on its own dataset. A row of the dataset pairs the features observed at day tt with the return realized over the subsequent hh days,

xt=(STRt,MTMt,LTRt),yt=rt+h,x_{t}=\left(\mathrm{STR}_{t},\,\mathrm{MTM}_{t},\,\mathrm{LTR}_{t}\right),\qquad y_{t}=r_{t+h}, (22)

so in our case F=3F=3. Stacking the rows over time gives the arrays X∈𝐑T×FX\in\mathbf{R}^{T\times F} and y∈𝐑Ty\in\mathbf{R}^{T}, one pair per asset.

At each forecasting date tt the coefficients are re-estimated from the HH most recent pairs whose outcome is known. A pair with feature date ss is complete only once its target rs+hr_{s+h} has been realized before the forecast is made, so the newest usable feature date is t−h−1t-h-1, and the split becomes

Xtrn=X[t−h−H:t−h−1],ytrn=y[t−h−H:t−h−1],xtst=xt,ytst=yt,X_{\mathrm{trn}}=X_{[t-h-H\,:\,t-h-1]},\qquad y_{\mathrm{trn}}=y_{[t-h-H\,:\,t-h-1]},\qquad x_{\mathrm{tst}}=x_{t},\qquad y_{\mathrm{tst}}=y_{t}, (23)

with Xtrn∈𝐑H×FX_{\mathrm{trn}}\in\mathbf{R}^{H\times F} and ytrn∈𝐑Hy_{\mathrm{trn}}\in\mathbf{R}^{H}. The gap of hh days between the last training pair and today is what keeps future information out of the fit. The features observed today, xtstx_{\mathrm{tst}}, are held out for the forecast, and their outcome ytsty_{\mathrm{tst}} is realized only hh days later, entering the evaluation of §6.3 but never the training sample.

The simplest estimate of θ\theta is ordinary least squares (OLS), which minimizes the squared prediction error over the training set. The simplicity is attractive but does not prevent overfitting. OLS is free to assign large coefficients to relationships that arose largely from noise, the problem grows as the number of parameters rises relative to the amount of training data, and correlated features make the estimates sensitive to small changes in the sample. We therefore use ridge regression, which adds an L2L_{2} penalty on the magnitude of the coefficients,

θ^=arg⁡minθ⁡‖ytrn−Xtrn​θ‖22+λ​‖θ‖22=(XtrnT​Xtrn+λ​IF)−1​XtrnT​ytrn,\hat{\theta}=\arg\min_{\theta}\,\|y_{\mathrm{trn}}-X_{\mathrm{trn}}\theta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\,\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}=\left(X_{\mathrm{trn}}^{\mathrm{T}}X_{\mathrm{trn}}+\lambda I_{F}\right)^{-1}X_{\mathrm{trn}}^{\mathrm{T}}\,y_{\mathrm{trn}}, (24)

where λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 sets the strength of the regularization and IFI_{F} is the identity matrix. The first equality defines the estimator and the second is its closed form solution. At λ=0\lambda=0 the penalty disappears and the solution reduces to OLS. As λ\lambda grows, large coefficients become progressively more costly, and a feature must show stronger evidence in the training data before it earns influence over the forecast. The shrinkage deliberately trades bias for lower estimation variance. A relationship that appears predictive only by chance would otherwise receive a large coefficient and swing as the training window moves forward, and ridge presses such coefficients toward zero. In the low signal-to-noise setting described above, a forecast near zero is not necessarily a failure. It can simply reflect that the data offers too little evidence for a stronger prediction.

The fitted coefficients applied to the held out features give the forecast, r^t+h=xtstT​θ^\hat{r}_{t+h}=x_{\mathrm{tst}}^{\mathrm{T}}\hat{\theta}, which directly or after a transformation is the alpha supplied to Markowitz. The closed form matters in practice. The model is re-estimated at every trading date, separately for every asset and specification, and avoiding iterative optimization keeps the cost of these repeated fits low. More flexible nonlinear models could capture relationships a linear model cannot, but they bring additional computational cost, more modeling choices, and greater capacity to fit the noise that already dominates the data. For our purposes ridge regression is the compromise between regularization, interpretability, and computational efficiency.

6 Numerical experiments

This section presents the numerical experiments that we have run to test the different trading strategies discussed above. We start by defining how our backtest is setup and runs. In §6.2 we give intuition behind the choice of ETFs for the simple trading strategies defined in §3.2. In §6.3 we evaluate the risk models presented in §4 and selection of alpha in §5. We end by showing the performance of a smaller set of reasonable portfolios and strategies derived from the conclusions of the previous sections.

6.1 Data and backtest

Data.

Daily adjusted close prices for all assets are sourced from Yahoo Finance [109] via the yfinance Python package [2]. Macroeconomic time series, such as the federal funds rate, are retrieved from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database [42] accessed via the fredapi package [108].

Backtest.

We evaluate our portfolio construction methods through a daily backtest covering 2005-01-01 to 2025-01-01, a total of T=5,032T=5{,}032 trading days t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T. Every trade in it is decided by one of the strategies of §3, and we consider the universe of nn assets of §2.1 plus cash. Let ht∈𝐑nh_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n} denote the dollar holdings in each asset and ct∈𝐑c_{t}\in\mathbf{R} the cash balance at the start of day tt. We allow no shorting and no leverage, so ht≥0h_{t}\geq 0 and ct≥0c_{t}\geq 0. The net asset value (NAV) and the portfolio weights are

vt=𝟏T​ht+ct,wt=ht/vt,v_{t}=\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}h_{t}+c_{t},\qquad w_{t}=h_{t}/v_{t},

with the remaining fraction 1−𝟏T​wt1-\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w_{t} held as cash. Each day the holdings drift with the realized return vector rt∈𝐑nr_{t}\in\mathbf{R}^{n} and cash earns the federal funds rate rf,tr_{f,t},

ht+1=diag⁡(1+rt)​ht,ct+1=(1+rf,t)​ct.h_{t+1}=\mathrm{diag}(1+r_{t})\,h_{t},\qquad c_{t+1}=(1+r_{f,t})\,c_{t}. (25)

On a day without trading this is the entire update. On a trading date, trades are assumed to execute at the start of day tt at the previous day’s closing price, after which holdings drift. Writing wp​r​ew_{pre} for the weights carried into the trade, the turnover on day tt is

τt=12​‖wt−wp​r​e‖1,\tau_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\|w_{t}-w_{pre}\|_{1}, (26)

so that moving capital out of one asset and into another counts once rather than twice. Every dollar bought or sold pays half of a bid-ask spread of κ=5\kappa=5 basis points, and the cost κ​τt​vt\kappa\,\tau_{t}\,v_{t} is deducted from cash. The Python code for the backtest loop and each of trading strategies it uses to update the portfolio weights can be found in Appendix 1 and 2.

Not every ETF in the universe of §2.1 was listed on the first day of the backtest, and the exact listing dates are given in Table 26. The backtest is simply not allowed to buy an asset before it was listed, so the number of assets a strategy can choose from grows over the period. We also require assets to have a minimum amount of 126 trading days before it becomes available, since the risk model and the return forecasts both need a trailing window of observations.

Evaluation.

We evaluate strategies using six performance metrics. These are the annualized geometric excess return rer_{e}, the annualized realized volatility σ\sigma, the maximum drawdown (MDD), the Sharpe ratio (SR), the average annual turnover (TO), and the lower quartile (LQ) of the per-year Sharpe ratio. Let rp,t∈𝐑r_{p,t}\in\mathbf{R} denote the realized portfolio return on day tt. We define rer_{e} and σ\sigma as,

re=(∏t=1T1+rp,t1+rf,t)252/T−1,σ=(252T​∑t=1T(rp,t−r¯p)2)1/2,r_{e}=\left(\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1+r_{p,t}}{1+r_{f,t}}\right)^{\!252/T}-1,\qquad\sigma=\left(\frac{252}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_{p,t}-\bar{r}_{p})^{2}\right)^{1/2}, (27)

where r¯p=(1/T)​∑t=1Trp,t\bar{r}_{p}=(1/T)\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{p,t} is the sample mean and the factor 252252 annualizes the per-period estimate under the assumption that daily returns are uncorrelated across time. The return is measured net of the risk-free rate while the volatility is measured on the portfolio return itself. We use the geometric mean because it equals the realized compound return, whereas the arithmetic mean overstates compound performance whenever returns vary [43]. We write MDD, SR, and LQ as,

MDD=max1≤t≤T⁡Dt,SR=reσ,LQ=Q0.25​({SRy}y),\mathrm{MDD}=\max_{1\leq t\leq T}D_{t},\qquad\mathrm{SR}=\frac{r_{e}}{\sigma},\qquad\mathrm{LQ}=Q_{0.25}\big(\{\mathrm{SR}_{y}\}_{y}\big), (28)

where Dt=max1≤τ≤t⁡(Vτ−Vt)/VτD_{t}=\max_{1\leq\tau\leq t}(V_{\tau}-V_{t})/V_{\tau} is the running drawdown at time tt, VtV_{t} is the portfolio NAV at time tt, MDD is the worst such drawdown over the backtest, and SRy\mathrm{SR}_{y} is the annualized Sharpe ratio within calendar year yy. LQ is the empirical 2525th percentile of the per-year Sharpe ratios and is our measure of weak-year consistency. Turnover is reported as the average over calendar years of ∑t∈yτt\sum_{t\in y}\tau_{t}, so a TO of 0.200.20 means that a fifth of the portfolio changed in a typical year.

Parameters.

The portfolio construction methods of §3 and the risk and alpha models of §4 and §5 introduce a number of free parameters. We fix these once and use the same values throughout, unless stated otherwise. None are finely tuned. In each case we take a round number within the range reported in the literature, rather than optimizing for any single metric. Table 3 lists the parameters central to the backtest and the trading strategies, while the remaining model parameters are given in §6.3.

6.2 Simple strategies

The simple strategies of §3.2 each need a smaller portfolio to run on. This section examines the candidate portfolios for each strategy. The strategies are ordered by complexity, and each addresses a specific shortcoming of the strategy before it. For each strategy we report what it addresses, our findings on portfolio composition, and which assets are reasonable to include.

Fixed weights.

We begin with equal weights. We backtest every combination of three, four, and five ETFs, rebalancing monthly, and rank the resulting portfolios twice: first by SR alone and then by SR followed by LQ. We exclude two groups of assets from the search. First, the Country and Futures categories, since they are not suitable buy-and-hold assets, as established in §2.2, and the fixed-weight strategy can do little beyond buying, holding, and rebalancing. Second, we exclude any ETF that was not listed at the start of the backtest. An investor in 2005 could not have selected an asset that did not yet exist, and introducing new ETFs as they became available would change the portfolio composition during the experiment. These restrictions leave 23 ETFs. Rather than testing every possible allocation for every combination, we initially restrict the search to equal weights. This separates two questions that would otherwise be mixed together: which assets should a fixed-weight portfolio contain, and how should capital be divided among them? Here we focus on the first question and return to the choice of proportions afterwards. Table 27 in the appendix reports the top 60 portfolios under both ranking criteria for each portfolio size, while Table 4 presents the best portfolios under each criterion.

The two ranking criteria favor somewhat different portfolios. When ranked by SR, the strongest portfolios combine an aggressive equity position, typically QQQ, with intermediate- or long-term government bonds such as IEF or TLT and an allocation to gold through GLD. These portfolios reach Sharpe ratios around 0.800.80–0.840.84 at roughly 8%8\%–9%9\% volatility, with maximum drawdowns around 19%19\%–22%22\%. Ranking by SR+LQ instead shifts the portfolios toward equities. For example, the highest-ranked three-ETF portfolio replaces the bond allocation with XLV, combining the growth-oriented XLK with a less volatile, defensive equity sector and gold. This shift comes at the cost of higher overall volatility and larger maximum drawdowns, but substantially improves LQ: compared with the top three-ETF portfolio ranked by SR, volatility rises from 9%9\% to 13%13\% and MDD from 22%22\% to 33%33\%, while LQ increases from 0.440.44 to 0.730.73. The difference reflects what the two consistency measures capture. LQ is based on the lower quartile of annual Sharpe ratios and therefore rewards portfolios that perform consistently across years, while a single extreme loss has limited influence on the measure. MDD behaves in the opposite way: it is determined entirely by the most severe peak-to-trough loss. Since the backtest contains three major market crashes, the two measures can therefore favor different portfolio compositions. Government bonds such as IEF and TLT provide protection during severe equity downturns and improve MDD, whereas replacing some of this protection with additional equity exposure, such as XLV or XLU, can improve performance across a larger share of individual years and therefore increase LQ.

Common characteristics.

Despite these differences, the strongest portfolios share a clear structure and generally draw from all three asset classes. Gold appears particularly consistently: GLD, the only Alternatives ETF with sufficient history to enter the search, is present in every one of the top fifteen portfolios at each portfolio size and in most of the remaining top 60. Fixed-income allocations are dominated by government bonds. Although the corporate bond ETF LQD occasionally appears, government bond alternatives rank higher for the same equity-and-gold combinations. The equity allocation, meanwhile, is typically concentrated in growth-oriented assets, with larger portfolios often adding either a defensive equity sector or a second government bond position. Adding more ETFs therefore provides only limited improvement. Moving from three to four or five assets increases the best Sharpe ratio only slightly, from 0.810.81 for three ETFs to 0.840.84 for both four and five ETFs, and the additional holdings are usually variations of exposures already present in the portfolio. The main result is consequently not a particular winning combination of ETFs, but a recurring allocation across distinct sources of risk: growth-oriented equities provide return, government bonds provide protection during equity downturns, and gold adds a third source of diversification.

Choosing the split.

The equal-weight search identifies which assets work well together, but leaves open whether their exact proportions matter. This is particularly relevant for fixed-weight portfolios such as the 60/40, where the allocation itself is part of the strategy. To isolate this effect, we select SPY, AGG, and GLD as representative ETFs for equities, fixed income, and alternatives, and backtest every allocation between them in ten-percentage-point increments. Table 28 in the appendix reports the full sweep, while Figure 18 shows the average allocation of the ten best-performing splits under each ranking criterion.

The results suggest that the exact allocation matters less than holding all three asset classes. When ranked by SR, the best-performing splits are centered close to an equal allocation between SPY, AGG, and GLD. Ranking by SR+LQ shifts some weight from gold toward equities, but the same three-way structure remains. The sweep also allows us to compare these portfolios directly with the traditional 60/40 portfolio. The 60/40 portfolio has a Sharpe ratio of 0.510.51 and a maximum drawdown of 0.360.36. By adding gold and adjusting the allocation across all three asset classes, the best portfolio with a 30/40/30 split increases the Sharpe ratio to 0.670.67 and reduces the maximum drawdown to 0.220.22.

Volatility control.

We next use the risk model to control the overall volatility of the portfolio. The simplest example is a portfolio containing only SPY. Figure 19 shows how the allocation between SPY and cash changes when an 8%8\% volatility target is applied.

The volatility control in (2) does not change the relative allocation between the assets in a portfolio. Instead, it scales the entire portfolio against cash until its estimated volatility reaches the target σtgt\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}. For SPY, this means investing more in the market when volatility is low and moving more of the portfolio into cash when volatility rises. This behavior is particularly visible during the turbulent periods of 2008–2009 and 2020–2021. Figure 20 compares SPY with its volatility-controlled counterpart during the three major market crashes in the backtest.

In all three crashes, volatility control reduces the drawdown by lowering market exposure as volatility increases. The trade-off is that the strategy can be slow to increase its exposure again once the market begins to recover, causing it to miss part of the rebound. This is particularly clear during the rapid recovery following the COVID-19 crash in the second panel. Table 28 in the appendix repeats the SPY/AGG/GLD allocation sweep with volatility control and shows three main effects. First, the strategy brings the realized risk of the different allocations much closer together. Without volatility control, realized volatility ranges from approximately 5%5\% to 17%17\%. With an 8%8\% target, the portfolios are instead limited to approximately this level, with deviations of around ±1%\pm 1\% due to errors in the risk forecast. Second, maximum drawdown decreases across the allocations, with the largest improvements occurring in the most aggressive portfolios. For example, the near-all-equity 90/0/10 allocation sees its maximum drawdown fall from 50%50\% to 20%20\%. Third, this reduction in risk does not necessarily come at the expense of the Sharpe ratio. The best allocation retains an SR of 0.670.67, while the SR of the 90/0/10 allocation increases from 0.500.50 to 0.570.57 as the volatility control reduces its exposure during the worst periods. Volatility control therefore provides a simple way to manage how much risk the portfolio takes, but it does not determine where that risk should come from. Since every holding is scaled by the same factor, the investor must still decide which assets to hold and how to allocate between them. The next strategy takes a step toward solving this problem by sizing each position according to its individual risk.

Inverse volatility.

Inverse volatility replaces the static allocation of fixed weights with an allocation that adapts to changes in risk. Under (3), each asset is weighted inversely to its estimated volatility, giving larger positions to less volatile assets and smaller positions to more volatile ones. These weights are recomputed at every trade, allowing the portfolio to adjust as market conditions change.

We first apply inverse volatility to the best equal-weight portfolios from the previous section. The results are shown in Table 5.

The main result is that inverse volatility works best when the assets have reasonably similar levels of volatility. In this case, no single asset dominates the allocation, but the weights can still adjust as their relative risks change. For example, TLT has a volatility of around 15%15\%, which is comparable to the equity and gold ETFs it is combined with. In portfolios containing TLT, inverse-volatility weighting improves the allocation: for QQQ/XLP/TLT/GLD, the Sharpe ratio increases from 0.840.84 under equal weights to 0.910.91, while LQ increases from 0.620.62 to 0.700.70. When all assets have very similar volatility, the inverse-volatility allocation instead remains close to equal weights and performance changes little. The weakness of the strategy appears when one asset is much less volatile than the others. Since a low volatility directly translates into a large weight, a sufficiently calm asset can dominate the portfolio. IEF, for example, has a volatility of around 7%7\% and receives roughly 60%60\% of QQQ/IEF/GLD. Although the Sharpe ratio increases slightly, the portfolio becomes much more dependent on bonds: annual return falls from 10%10\% to 7%7\%, while LQ falls from 0.440.44 to 0.210.21. The same problem is even more pronounced for low-volatility assets such as AGG. Inverse volatility therefore does not necessarily favor the asset that provides the most useful diversification; it simply favors the asset with the lowest individual volatility.

To see whether this pattern holds more generally, we repeat the exhaustive search using inverse-volatility weights. The top 60 portfolios for each portfolio size are reported in Table 29. The same broad portfolio structure found under equal weights remains: the strongest portfolios combine growth-oriented equities, defensive equities, government bonds, and gold. However, the best Sharpe ratios increase from 0.810.81, 0.840.84, and 0.840.84 under equal weights to 0.840.84, 0.910.91, and 0.900.90 under inverse volatility for portfolios of three, four, and five ETFs, respectively. TLT also performs better in these portfolios than lower-volatility aggregate bonds, supporting the earlier result that inverse volatility is most effective when the assets provide different sources of risk without having vastly different volatility levels. This leads to the main limitation of inverse volatility: it considers each asset separately. The strategy knows how volatile an asset is, but not whether it moves together with the other assets in the portfolio. Adding several similar equity ETFs therefore gives each of them its own allocation and can unintentionally increase the portfolio’s total equity exposure. Likewise, including a very low-volatility bond ETF can cause fixed income to dominate the portfolio. Inverse volatility can determine the size of each position, but it cannot determine which assets should be held together. The remaining strategies address this limitation by using the full covariance structure, allowing both individual risk and the relationships between assets to influence the allocation.

Minimum volatility.

Minimum volatility of (4) is the first strategy to use the full covariance matrix, which addresses exactly what inverse volatility lacked. It can distinguish a diversifying asset from a duplicate. What it cannot see is return, and this section shows both sides of that trade-off. We run it through three tests that the two remaining strategies will repeat, a duplicate asset, a set of complementary assets, and an extreme asset. Table 6 starts with SPY and AGG, the assets of the 60/40, and then adds VTV and VUG.

AGG has a volatility of 5%5\% against SPY’s 19%19\%, and with no notion of return, minimum volatility holds the pair in a near 10/90 split, as seen in Figure 21.

The portfolio earns 4%4\% per year at a Sharpe ratio of 0.380.38, well below the 0.510.51 of the fixed 60/40 split of the same two assets. This is the concentration problem described in §3.2. Adding VTV and VUG changes almost nothing since minimum volatility recognizes that the three equities are highly correlated and splits the same small allocation between them.

The concentration in AGG comes from the asset selection as much as from the method, since AGG is the only low volatility asset available. Table 7 instead replaces AGG with TLT and GLD, complementary assets whose volatilities are closer to SPY’s.

With similar volatilities their covariance decides the allocation. TLT with SPY raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.380.38 to 0.650.65 and GLD with SPY reaches 0.700.70, and combining all three reaches 0.870.87 with an LQ of 0.560.56, on par with the best equal weight portfolios. Minimum volatility thus finds good proportions within complementary assets of similar risk, and can be trusted with more, as USMV of §3.2 shows on US stocks.

In the last experiment we add IBIT, the bitcoin ETF extended back to 2017 as described in §2.2. Table 8 shows the result.

Nothing changes. To an objective that only minimizes risk, bitcoin is only risk, and the optimizer sets the position to zero. The next strategy instead enforces a more equal split of the risk.

Risk parity.

Risk parity uses the same covariance matrix but with a different objective. The formulation in (5) forces every asset to contribute the same share of the total portfolio risk, so no asset can be dropped and no asset can dominate. We run the same three tests, starting with the duplicates in Table 9.

The equal risk condition changes both rows. SPY and AGG now split the risk evenly instead of the capital, which gives SPY a meaningful weight and raises the Sharpe ratio from minimum volatility’s 0.380.38 to 0.580.58. Adding VTV and VUG shows how risk parity handles more assets of similar risk profile. Each equity claims its own equal share, so three quarters of the portfolio risk now comes from equities, as seen in Figure 22.

Volatility, however, rises from 6%6\% to 8%8\%. The problem that was present in inverse volatility returns, now in risk rather than in capital. Table 10 repeats the complementary asset test.

The notable rows are the ones holding AGG. Since no asset can contribute more than its equal share of the risk, the low volatility bond can no longer dominate, and risk parity is the first strategy where AGG improves the portfolio. SPY/AGG/GLD reaches a Sharpe ratio of 0.740.74 with an LQ of 0.640.64, the most consistent of the SPY portfolios in these tests. Replacing AGG with TLT raises the Sharpe ratio to 0.790.79 but LQ falls to 0.250.25, so we keep the AGG version for the final test in Table 11.

Where minimum volatility excluded bitcoin, risk parity must hold it, and the equal risk condition decides how much. IBIT enters at a weight of a few percent, and since bitcoin is nearly uncorrelated with the rest, the Sharpe ratio rises from 0.740.74 to 0.840.84 and LQ from 0.640.64 to 0.720.72. Being forced to hold every asset, works in the investor’s favor here, but the same rule means risk parity would, if allowed, also hold the futures ETFs of §2.2. The final strategy can again exclude assets, this time for being redundant rather than volatile.

Maximum diversification.

Maximum diversification also uses the full covariance matrix as minimum volatility and risk parity but instead seeks the portfolio where combining assets results in the largest diversification ratio of (6). The reformulation in (7) is solved on the correlation matrix, with every asset scaled by its own volatility beforehand, so the volatility of an asset no longer decides how much of it is held. Table 12 starts with the duplicate test.

The strategy allocates its capital in a unique way. VTV and VUG together essentially form SPY, and to the diversification ratio the two parts are the marginally more diversified way of holding the same exposure, so SPY is dropped as redundant, as seen in Figure 23.

Performance is close to unchanged, which is expected. The strategy holds the same exposure through different tickers. The SPY/AGG pair is also worth noting. It reaches a Sharpe ratio of 0.520.52 against minimum volatility’s 0.380.38, because the objective works on correlations rather than volatilities, so AGG no longer dominates the portfolio even though it is still the only low volatility asset available. Table 13 repeats the complementary asset test.

Which bond sits next to SPY matters much less than before. Under minimum volatility, SPY/AGG achives a Sharpe ratio of 0.380.38 and SPY/TLT 0.650.65, a gap driven almost entirely by their volatility levels. Here the same pair of portfolios achieve 0.520.52 and 0.640.64, and the remaining difference comes from correlation. TLT has a correlation of −0.32-0.32 with SPY against AGG’s −0.01-0.01 in Table 26, and a negative correlation is exactly what the diversification ratio rewards, so the strategy still prefers TLT, but now for a better reason. Adding GLD completes the trio, and SPY/TLT/GLD reaches a Sharpe ratio of 0.820.82. Table 14 adds IBIT.

This is the setting the strategy was built for. IBIT is close to uncorrelated with everything else in the universe, which is exactly what the objective rewards, and because every asset is scaled by its own volatility, the position stays small on its own. Nothing forces the strategy to hold bitcoin, as risk parity did, and nothing caps the position, as minimum volatility effectively did by excluding it. The optimizer simply holds a small amount because it improves the portfolio, and the Sharpe ratio rises from 0.820.82 to 0.900.90 with LQ unchanged.

Every portfolio so far has used a smaller subset of assets. The last question is whether the strategy can be trusted with a larger selection, which minimum volatility and risk parity could not. As a test, we hand maximum diversification all 30 ETFs in the Market, Sector, Government, Physical, and Crypto categories, the same categories we previously included in the exhaustive search. No three to five ETFs are chosen, instead the strategy gets everything in each category and must find the allocation on its own. Table 15 reports the result.

It works. The strategy holds a broad mix across the asset classes throughout, as seen in Figure 24, and delivers a Sharpe ratio of 0.730.73 on a selection where minimum volatility would have concentrated in the lowest volatility bonds. The cost is turnover. Rebalancing thirty positions every month turns the portfolio over one and a half times per year, and the smaller selected portfolios above reach higher Sharpe ratios at a fraction of the effort. Selecting at the category level is possible, but for an investor willing to pick a handful of ETFs, it is not worth the trading.

Finally, for the curious reader, we show the portfolio of five assets that achieved the highest Sharpe ratio for any simple strategy we found. This portfolio used maximum diversification, and the assets included is not far from what we consider to be reasonable. The portfolio and related metrics can be seen in Table 16.

QQQ and XLP as offensive and defensive equities, TLT, GLD, and a small position in IBIT, weighted by maximum diversification, reach a Sharpe ratio of 1.021.02 with an LQ of 0.600.60. We report this combination as a reference rather than propose it, since it was found by searching over the backtest period itself, and its performance is therefore a product of hindsight. It nevertheless summarizes the section well. The best simple portfolios keep returning to the same core concept. The concept being, two equities that complement each other, a long term bond, gold, and a small position in an uncorrelated extreme asset such as bitcoin, held together by a rule that uses the full covariance matrix. Simple and implementable. However, there is more to portfolio construction. Every strategy in this section is blind to return, which is why the assets had to be picked by hand, with no futures and no single country funds among them. The Markowitz formulation of §3.3 removes that restriction by letting a forecast decide which assets are worth holding, and the next two sections cover the two forecasts it needs, including the covariance matrix that has been trated as given in this section above.

6.3 Risk and alpha model

Before the portfolio backtests of §6.4 we evaluate the two forecasts on their own. Following [52], a forecast can be judged directly, by statistical measures of how well it describes the quantity it predicts, or indirectly, by the performance of the portfolios built on it. This section does the former, and states the parameter values used for each model.

Risk model.

We first fix the number of factors for the factor model of §4 by examining the cumulative share of variance explained by the leading principal components. The first component alone explains half of all variance in the universe, which can be interpreted as the market factor, and the first ten explain 89%89\%, after which each additional component adds around one percentage point. We use k=10k=10 throughout. Table 17 lists all of the relevant risk model parameters.

We evaluate our covariance forecast against the true realized volatility. At the end of each month every model produces a forecast Σ^t\hat{\Sigma}_{t}, and the target is the realized covariance Σt\Sigma_{t} of the following 21 trading days, since we trade monthly. The distance between the two is the Frobenius norm, relative to the magnitude of the target,

‖A‖F=(∑i∑jAi​j2)1/2,dt=‖Σ^t−Σt‖F‖Σt‖F,\|A\|_{\mathrm{F}}=\Big(\sum_{i}\sum_{j}A_{ij}^{2}\Big)^{1/2},\qquad d_{t}=\frac{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{t}-\Sigma_{t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}}{\|\Sigma_{t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}},

so the empty forecast Σ^t=0\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=0 scores exactly one, a perfect forecast zero, and the reported value is the fraction of the realized covariance the model fails to capture. Table 18 reports the average of dtd_{t} over the backtest for each model.

The factor model performs better for every asset class and over the full universe, but the gain is marginal, and all three models leave roughly a fifth of the realized covariance unexplained. For a small universe of, say, three assets, either simple estimator is a fully reasonable substitute for the factor model. We, nevertheless, use the factor model proposed in all experiments above in §6.2 and that follow.

Regression model.

The regression forecasts of §5.3 are evaluated out of sample. At each trading date the model is fitted on the trailing window, using the parameters of Table 19, which is then used our prediction of returns for the following period.

The predictions r^t\hat{r}_{t} are then compared with the actual realized returns rtr_{t} through the out-of-sample R2R^{2},

R2=1−∑t(rt−r^t)2∑trt2.R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{t}(r_{t}-\hat{r}_{t})^{2}}{\sum_{t}r_{t}^{2}}.

Since returns are treated as zero mean, the denominator is the error of the forecast that always predicts zero. This gives us that a R2=1R^{2}=1 represents a perfect forecast, while a R2=0R^{2}=0 is exactly as good as always saying zero, and R2<0R^{2}<0 is worse than saying nothing at all. To evaluate the importance of the regulization parameterλ\lambda, we sweep it across several orders of magnitude and evaluate the model at each level. Figure 25 shows the result, reporting the mean R2R^{2} across all ETFs with one standard deviation plotted with dashed lines.

Every entry in the figure is negative, so at no level of regularization does the model beat the zero forecast for a single asset. The R2R^{2} nevertheless improves as the regularization grows, since increasing λ\lambda shrinks the coefficients and thus the predictions toward zero, whose R2R^{2} is zero by construction. This matters for how the forecast should be judged. A portfolio built on the model may well backtest decently, but a model whose statistical score improves only as it regularizes away its parameters offers no evidence that such performance is more than noise. We therefore conclude that our attempts at fitting a model bear no statistical support, though this does not mean return prediction is impossible. Our code is open for the reader to search for statistical support themselves, but at this point we defer to Markowitz’s own words when asked about estimating expected returns, “That’s your job, not mine” [16].

Simple signals.

The simple signals of §5.2, with parameters given in Table 20, cannot be scored with the out-of-sample R2R^{2} above. The moving average only takes the values ±1\pm 1 and momentum only assumes that recent returns persist, so neither makes a claim about the size of future returns.

We therefore evaluate them indirectly, through the performance of the portfolios they build. Each signal is run through the Markowitz problem of §3.3 on the full universe of §2.1, first with every asset receiving the one-month momentum signal, then with every asset receiving the moving average signal. Table 21 reports both.

Both portfolios perform considerably worse than the simple strategies of §6.2. The Sharpe ratios of 0.430.43 and 0.450.45 are roughly those of holding SPY alone, and both portfolios trade more than their full value in a typical year. The momentum is always invested somewhere and its LQ of −0.03-0.03 means its weak years do not beat cash, while the moving average keeps an LQ of 0.480.48, since it moves the portfolio into cash when few assets are trending. A likely explanation is the universe itself, which still contains the categories that §2.2 argued against holding, and a monthly signal under the turnover limits of (10) cannot always keep them out. We therefore run an ablation test, removing one category at a time and rerunning the entire backtest, nine runs per signal. Tables 22 and 23 report the results, with the categories we later remove highlighted in grey.

Each row is the full universe with one category removed, so a Sharpe ratio above the 0.450.45 and 0.430.43 baselines means the category hurt the overall performance. For momentum, removing Futures gives the largest improvement, to 0.530.53, and removing Countries the second largest, to 0.510.51. Countries is the only category whose removal improves both signals, in line with Figure 7. The improvement from removing Sectors, to 0.470.47, is the one result we did not expect. A possible explanation is that sectors that trend have larger drawdowns that a one-month window cannot anticipate. At the other end, removing Crypto lowers the Sharpe ratio to 0.290.29, the largest change in either test. Momentum works best on assets with strong trends, and bitcoin has clearly had strong trends.

For the moving average, removing Countries, Government, or Global improves the portfolio, while removing Market or Sectors makes it worse. The signal handles bonds poorly since a signal that only asks whether the price is above its trend gives a bond ETF returning 3%3\% little to no room for inclusion. We remove the highlighted categories and rerun both portfolios. Table 24 shows both portfolios after the removals.

Momentum improves substantially. The Sharpe ratio rises from 0.430.43 to 0.780.78, the drawdown falls from 0.200.20 to 0.160.16, LQ rises from −0.03-0.03 to 0.400.40, and turnover falls to 0.810.81, still several times that of the simple strategies. The moving average improves to 0.510.51 while its LQ falls from 0.480.48 to 0.300.30. The removals were chosen using the backtest results themselves, so some of the improvement is still due to selection. However, Futures and Countries were argued against in §2.2 on structural grounds, before any backtest was run. We therefore consider the selection bias introduced by the ablation to be modest, though not zero. Momentum is also a standard signal in industry practice [83], and its resulting portfolio holds 26 ETFs across six categories, with no individual asset selected by hand. We call this the Momentum Universe and carry it to §6.4.

6.4 Proposed portfolios

From the experiments above we propose four portfolios, listed in increasing order of the involvement they demand of the investor. SPY under 8% volatility control, SPY/AGG/GLD in an equal weight split, SPY/TLT/GLD/IBIT under maximum diversification, and the Momentum Universe of §6.3 under Markowitz. We benchmark against the 60/40, and the regret bound of §3.3 marks an upper bound. Figure 26 shows the growth of each portfolio and Table 25 reports the metrics. Table 30 in the appendix repeats them over two truncated windows, and the ordering between the portfolios holds.

7 Conclusions

This paper studied portfolio construction from the perspective of the private investor. All methods were evaluated under the same setting: 59 liquid US ETFs, no shorting or leverage, monthly trading with a 5 basis point spread, an 8% volatility target, and data from 2005–2025, with no parameters tuned to the evaluation period. Under these conditions, simple portfolios containing as few as three ETFs achieve consistent and decent returns, and the portfolios we propose outperform the 60/40 benchmark.

The clearest result concerns asset selection. The strongest simple portfolios combine growth-oriented equities, government bonds, and gold, while the exact allocation appears less important than including all three. An equally weighted portfolio of SPY, AGG, and GLD raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.52 for the 60/40 to 0.68 and reduces maximum drawdown from 30% to 24%, while requiring only one additional asset.

The simple strategies also perform well relative to more sophisticated alternatives. Fixed weights is difficult to improve upon for a well-chosen set of ETFs, while volatility control provides a direct and interpretable way to manage risk. The optimization-based strategies offer different advantages depending on the assets included. Minimum volatility is most suitable for complementary assets with comparable risk, while risk parity handles large differences in volatility more naturally. Maximum diversification is better suited to broader universes with more varied correlation structures. The strongest portfolio we propose uses maximum diversification across SPY, TLT, GLD, and IBIT, achieving a Sharpe ratio of 0.90.

The risk and alpha models lead to different conclusions. Risk forecasting proved useful, with the factor model producing the strongest covariance estimates, closely followed by simpler estimators. Return forecasting was demonstrated within the same simple and transparent framework, using only publicly available price data rather than proprietary information. In this setting, ridge regression never outperforms the zero forecast out of sample and improves only as regularization shrinks its predictions toward zero. This does not rule out richer return models or data sources, but highlights the difficulty of extracting predictive information from price history alone. The simpler momentum signal, when applied to a restricted universe, allows the Markowitz portfolio to achieve a Sharpe ratio of 0.78 and the smallest maximum drawdown among the proposed portfolios, although with substantially higher turnover. Markowitz also reduces the need to select individual ETFs in advance beyond broad asset categories.

These results should be interpreted with some considerations in mind. All performance is historical, the ETF universe is survivorship biased, and some use of prior knowledge when defining the universe is unavoidable. A strategy with perfect knowledge of future returns and yearly rebalancing achieves a Sharpe ratio of 1.57, as shown by the regret bound. The sensitivity analysis shows that the proposed portfolios do not depend on a single market crisis, although the relative performance of the 60/40 improves when the Financial Crisis is excluded. Finally, the framework relies entirely on public data, open-source code, and interpretable parameters, allowing the results to be reproduced and extended.

Appendix A Mathematical derivations

Derivation of the MDP QP formulation

From the original formulation of the MDP in (6), we rewrite y=Dσ​wy=D_{\sigma}w, where σ2=diag⁡(Σ)\sigma^{2}=\operatorname{diag}\,(\Sigma) and Dσ=diag⁡(σ)D_{\sigma}=\operatorname{diag}\,(\sigma). Substituting w=Dσ−1​yw=D^{-1}_{\sigma}y gives,

wT​σwT​Σ​w=(Dσ−1​y)T​σ(Dσ−1​y)T​Σ​(Dσ−1​y)=𝟏T​yyT​(Dσ−1​Σ​Dσ−1)​y=𝟏T​yyT​C​y,\frac{w^{\mathrm{T}}\sigma}{\sqrt{w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w}}=\frac{(D_{\sigma}^{-1}y)^{\mathrm{T}}\sigma}{\sqrt{(D_{\sigma}^{-1}y)^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma(D_{\sigma}^{-1}y)}}=\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y}{\sqrt{y^{\mathrm{T}}(D_{\sigma}^{-1}\Sigma D_{\sigma}^{-1})y}}=\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y}{\sqrt{y^{\mathrm{T}}Cy}},

and the constraint 𝟏T​w=𝟏T​(Dσ−1​y)\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w=\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}(D_{\sigma}^{-1}y). The objective is scale invariant with respect to ww, letting us scale the constraint 𝟏T​w\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}w to become 𝟏T​(Dσ​w)=𝟏T​(Dσ​Dσ−1​y)=𝟏T​y\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}(D_{\sigma}w)=\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}(D_{\sigma}D_{\sigma}^{-1}y)=\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y before solving for yy and then rescaling the solution back to ww. We reformulate the optimization problem with the new constraints as,

maximize𝑦\displaystyle\underset{y}{\text{maximize}} 𝟏T​yyT​C​y\displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y}{\sqrt{y^{\mathrm{T}}Cy}}
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Ty=1,y≥0.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y=1,\quad y\geq 0.

The new constraint fixes the numerator, making this maximization problem equivalent to minimizing the denominator. This gives the final formulation,

minimize𝑦\displaystyle\underset{y}{\text{minimize}} yT​C​y\displaystyle y^{\mathrm{T}}Cy
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝟏Ty=1,y≥0.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}y=1,\quad y\geq 0.

After solving for y∗y^{*}, undo the change of variables and normalize,

w∗=Dσ−1​y∗𝟏T​Dσ−1​y∗.w^{*}=\frac{D^{-1}_{\sigma}y^{*}}{\mathbf{1}^{\mathrm{T}}D^{-1}_{\sigma}y^{*}}.

Derivation of the factor model decomposition

Consider the factor model

r=F​f+ϵ,r=Ff+\epsilon,

with 𝐄⁡[f]=0\mathbf{E}[f]=0, 𝐄⁡[ϵ]=0\mathbf{E}[\epsilon]=0, Cov⁡(f,ϵ)=0\operatorname{Cov}(f,\epsilon)=0, and Cov⁡(f)=Ik\operatorname{Cov}(f)=I_{k}. Taking the covariance gives

Σ\displaystyle\Sigma =Cov⁡(F​f+ϵ)\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}(Ff+\epsilon)
=F​Cov⁡(f)​FT+Cov⁡(ϵ)\displaystyle=F\operatorname{Cov}(f)F^{\mathrm{T}}+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon)
=F​FT+D,\displaystyle=FF^{\mathrm{T}}+D,

where the cross-covariance terms vanish because Cov⁡(f,ϵ)=0\operatorname{Cov}(f,\epsilon)=0. Assuming that the idiosyncratic returns are mutually uncorrelated gives

D=Cov⁡(ϵ)=diag⁡(σ12,…,σn2).D=\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon)=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{n}^{2}).

Hence,

Σ=F​FT+D.\Sigma=FF^{\mathrm{T}}+D.

Estimation of the statistical factor model

At each time tt, the factor model is estimated from the historical return matrix RtR_{t}. Let

Dσ,t=diag⁡(σ^1,t,…,σ^n,t)D_{\sigma,t}=\operatorname{diag}(\hat{\sigma}_{1,t},\ldots,\hat{\sigma}_{n,t})

contain the EWMA volatility estimates with half-life HvarH_{\mathrm{var}}. After winsorization, the returns are standardized as

R~t=Rt​Dσ,t−1.\tilde{R}_{t}=R_{t}D_{\sigma,t}^{-1}.

Using the EWMA weighting matrix WtW_{t} with half-life HcovH_{\mathrm{cov}}, the weighted second-moment matrix is

St=R~tT​Wt​R~t.S_{t}=\tilde{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}W_{t}\tilde{R}_{t}.

Because the volatility and correlation estimates use separate EWMA half-lives, the diagonal of StS_{t} is not necessarily equal to one. We therefore normalize it to obtain the correlation matrix

Ct=DS,t−1​St​DS,t−1,DS,t=diag⁡(St)1/2.C_{t}=D_{S,t}^{-1}S_{t}D_{S,t}^{-1},\qquad D_{S,t}=\operatorname{diag}(S_{t})^{1/2}.

The EM algorithm is initialized from the leading kk eigenpairs of

Ct=Qt​Λt​QtT.C_{t}=Q_{t}\Lambda_{t}Q_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}.

Retaining the leading kk components gives

F0,t=Qk,t​Λk,t1/2,D0,t=diag⁡(Ct−F0,t​F0,tT).F_{0,t}=Q_{k,t}\Lambda_{k,t}^{1/2},\qquad D_{0,t}=\operatorname{diag}\left(C_{t}-F_{0,t}F_{0,t}^{\mathrm{T}}\right).

The factor loading matrix is the rank-kk approximation of the correlation structure, while D0,tD_{0,t} contains the residual diagonal variance. Starting from (F0,t,D0,t)(F_{0,t},D_{0,t}), the EM updates in below produce the fitted correlation decomposition

Ct≈Ft∗​Ft∗T+Dt∗.C_{t}\approx F_{t}^{*}F_{t}^{*\mathrm{T}}+D_{t}^{*}.

Finally, the decomposition is returned to the original volatility scale:

Ft=Dσ,t​Ft∗,Dt=Dσ,t​Dt∗​Dσ,t,F_{t}=D_{\sigma,t}F_{t}^{*},\qquad D_{t}=D_{\sigma,t}D_{t}^{*}D_{\sigma,t},

which gives the covariance forecast

Σ^t=Ft​FtT+Dt.\hat{\Sigma}_{t}=F_{t}F_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}+D_{t}.

Derivation of the EM updates for factor analysis

Given the correlation matrix CtC_{t}, we seek the maximum-likelihood estimates of (F,D)(F,D) under the factor model

r=F​f+ϵ,f∼𝒩⁡(0,Ik),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,D),r=Ff+\epsilon,\qquad f\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}),\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,D),

where DD is diagonal. Since the factors ff are latent, we estimate (F,D)(F,D) using the EM algorithm [34, 90].

E-step.

For a current estimate (F(j),D(j))(F^{(j)},D^{(j)}), define

G(j)=(Ik+F(j)​T​D(j)−1​F(j))−1,L(j)=G(j)​F(j)​T​D(j)−1.G^{(j)}=\left(I_{k}+F^{(j)\mathrm{T}}D^{(j)-1}F^{(j)}\right)^{-1},\qquad L^{(j)}=G^{(j)}F^{(j)\mathrm{T}}D^{(j)-1}.

Under the joint Gaussian model, the conditional moments of the latent factors are

𝐄⁡[f∣r]=L(j)​r,Cov⁡(f∣r)=G(j).\mathbf{E}[f\mid r]=L^{(j)}r,\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(f\mid r)=G^{(j)}.

Using the input correlation matrix CtC_{t} from Appendix A, the corresponding cross-moment and factor second moment are

Mr​f(j)=Ct​L(j)​T,Mf​f(j)=L(j)​Ct​L(j)​T+G(j).M_{rf}^{(j)}=C_{t}L^{(j)\mathrm{T}},\qquad M_{ff}^{(j)}=L^{(j)}C_{t}L^{(j)\mathrm{T}}+G^{(j)}.

M-step.

Holding these conditional moments fixed, maximizing the expected complete-data log-likelihood gives

F(j+1)=Mr​f(j)​(Mf​f(j))−1,F^{(j+1)}=M_{rf}^{(j)}\left(M_{ff}^{(j)}\right)^{-1},

followed by

D(j+1)=diag⁡(Ct−2​Mr​f(j)​F(j+1)​T+F(j+1)​Mf​f(j)​F(j+1)​T).D^{(j+1)}=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(C_{t}-2M_{rf}^{(j)}F^{(j+1)\mathrm{T}}+F^{(j+1)}M_{ff}^{(j)}F^{(j+1)\mathrm{T}}\right).

The diagonal restriction on DD allows each asset to have its own idiosyncratic variance while assuming that idiosyncratic returns are uncorrelated across assets.

Initialization and termination.

The algorithm is initialized using the rank-kk eigendecomposition described in Appendix A. The iterations continue until the relative changes in both FF and DD fall below a tolerance τ\tau,

‖F(j+1)−F(j)‖F‖F(j)‖F<τ,‖D(j+1)−D(j)‖F‖D(j)‖F<τ.\frac{\|F^{(j+1)}-F^{(j)}\|_{F}}{\|F^{(j)}\|_{F}}<\tau,\qquad\frac{\|D^{(j+1)}-D^{(j)}\|_{F}}{\|D^{(j)}\|_{F}}<\tau.

Appendix B Tables

Appendix C Code

Throughout this project several million backtests have been run, most of which solve one convex problem per trading date. We first present code examples that illustrate how the backtest and our trading strategies are implemented in Python. We then collect some of the implementation choices that made this scale possible, which together reduced the running time of the exhaustive search from days to under an hour.

The backtest loop

A backtest is a loop over trading days, and everything inside the loop should be plain vector and matrix operations. We load the adjusted closing prices once, convert them to a return matrix R∈𝐑T×nR\in\mathbf{R}^{T\times n}, and from that point on touch only NumPy arrays. Labeled data structures such as pandas dataframes are convenient but slow because of their per-operation overhead which dominates execution time. Restricting pandas to the boundary of the program and running the loop on NumPy arrays sped up each computed backtest by roughly 2 times. Listing 1 shows the loop in full.

The strategies

Inside construct_portfolio each strategy is a few lines of code, and all of the strategies of §3 are given in Listing 2. The formula-based ones are plain NumPy, and the optimization-based ones are direct transcriptions of their formulations into CVXPY.

Two formulation habits

Both of the following are standard advice in the convex optimization literature, and both transfer directly to portfolio problems. First, risk is better expressed through a norm than through a quadratic form. The constraint wT​Σ​w≤σtgt2w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}^{2} and the constraint ‖LT​w‖2≤σtgt\|L^{\mathrm{T}}w\|_{2}\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}, with LL the Cholesky factor of Σ\Sigma, describe the same set, but the norm version hands the solver a second-order cone directly and avoids squaring the conditioning of the problem. When the covariance comes from the factor model of §4.3, the full matrix F​Σf​FT+DF\Sigma^{f}F^{\mathrm{T}}+D should never be assembled. The portfolio variance splits into a factor part and an idiosyncratic part,

wT​Σ​w=‖F~T​w‖22+‖D1/2​w‖22,w^{\mathrm{T}}\Sigma w=\|\,\tilde{F}^{\mathrm{T}}w\,\|_{2}^{2}+\|\,D^{1/2}w\,\|_{2}^{2},

where F~=F​Lf\tilde{F}=FL_{f} and LfL_{f} is the Cholesky factor of Σf\Sigma^{f}, so the risk constraint involves one kk-vector and one nn-vector rather than an n×nn\times n matrix. This is the form used in Listing 2. At n=59n=59 the saving is modest, but the formulation costs nothing, and it is the version that scales as the universe grows.

Parallelism

A single backtest is serial, since the holdings on day tt depend on those on day t−1t-1. The backtests themselves are independent of each other, so we run them in parallel. We use a pool of twelve worker processes, one per core. Processes rather than threads, since Python’s global interpreter lock prevents threads from running Python code simultaneously. The price data is loaded and sliced once before the pool starts, so each worker only receives the arrays its own backtest needs.

Going faster

The setup above is fast enough for everything in this paper. If it were not, the same parametrized problems can be compiled. CVXPYgen [92] generates custom C code for a fixed problem structure, removing the remaining Python overhead from each solve, and slots into the loop with an unchanged interface. We did not need it for the results reported here, but for a larger universe, more frequent trading, or a wider hyperparameter sweep, it is the natural next step.

Appendix D For the European investor

This paper only considers ETFs that are accessible to American investors. Since January 2018, EU regulation requires any fund sold to European retail investors to provide a key information document [37], which US-listed ETFs do not have. The ETFs in this report can therefore not be bought through an ordinary European brokerage account. Equivalents are instead available through European UCITS funds that track the same or closely related indices. Table 31 lists the most relevant ETFs in this paper together with a European equivalent.

Several UCITS funds often track the same index. The funds listed here were selected because they are available through Avanza, a large Swedish online brokerage, so that a private investor can buy them directly. Other brokers may list other lines of the same fund, and the ISIN rather than the ticker is what identifies it.

The backtests of this paper assume that dividends are reinvested. This corresponds to an accumulating share class, marked (Acc), which reinvests the dividends inside the fund. Not every broker or fund offers this, and where we could not find an (Acc) equivalent we list the distributing class, marked (Dist), which pays the dividends out to the investor instead. The resulting return on your investment is mostly the same assuming you reinvest the dividends that is paid out. It does, however, affect what the price chart shows. The quoted price of a distributing fund usually excludes the dividends already paid out, so its growth may appear weaker than the return that is actually delivered.
